title: Comments
text:
Describing your process with comments
Comments can be helpful for briefly describing what the following code does.

# Subtract 1 from 10, then divide by 2
(10 - 1) / 2

[1] 4.5

# Take the sine of 3
sin(3)

[1] 0.14112



Comment on every line is not necessary
As code gets more complex, comments can help you figure out your process

title: Comments
text:
Better use of comments

Use comments to explain the why of your code

 

Think of it as note-taking for your future self and others who might read your code

In theory, we should be able to figure out what we were doing
So we want to leave ourselves notes about why we were doing it, and any important details that might not be obvious from the code itself


 

For example:


# Calculate average age of 3 people
(29 + 42 + 68) / 3

[1] 46.33333

title: Objects
text:
R objects are stored “things” in R
R objects can be data, numbers, text, model output, etc.
R objects are created with assignments that can be used in later commands

title: Objects
section: How can we create an object?
text:
How can we create an object?
Here is the generic way we assign something like a value to an object_name:
 

object_name <- value

 

Reads as “object name gets value” or “value is assigned to object name”

title: Objects
section: A note on the assignment operator
text:
A note on the assignment operator

Can assign a variable using either = or <-

Using <- is preferable for certain occasions
I usually just use = because less typing hehe



x = 5
x

[1] 5

text:
Another way to load (and install) packages: pacman

pacman::p_load(dplyr)

title: Data transformation: Basics
text:
dplyr basics

dplyr is a package in the tidyverse that provides a set of functions for data manipulation and transformation
Each function in dplyr serves almost like a verb that describes the action being performed on the data
Most functions within dplyr have similar input and output:

Input: a data frame (usually the first argument in the function)
Output: a data frame
Additional arguments: typically describe what columns (variables) to operate on

title: Data transformation: Basics
text:
Types of dplyr functions
dplyr functions can be categorized into four groups based on what they operate on:

rows: functions that operate on rows of a data frame (e.g., filter(), slice())
columns: functions that operate on columns of a data frame (e.g., select(), mutate())
groups: functions that operate on groups of rows in a data frame (e.g., group_by(), summarize())
joins: functions that combine two data frames based on a common key (e.g., left_join(), inner_join())

Not covering in this class (You can take BSTA 526 to learn about joins)

title: Lesson 4: Calling Functions
text:
R has many built-in functions that allow you to perform a variety of tasks
Functions usually take the form:


1function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )


1

function_name is the name of the function we are using. function_output

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.








seq() is a function that generates a sequence of numbers.
It has three arguments: from, to, and by
Output will be the sequence numbers


seq(
  from = 1, 
  to = 10, 
  by = 2
)

[1] 1 3 5 7 9






seq(1, 10, 2)

[1] 1 3 5 7 9






We can also assign the output of a function to an object using the assignment operator <-:


function_output <- function_name(
  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )


The output will not print, but it will be stored in the object function_output





We will assign the output of the seq() function to an object called odds:


odds <- seq(
  from = 1, 
  to = 10, 
  by = 2
)


So odds will now contain the sequence (1,3,5,7,9)

## Meet the penguins

The `penguins` data contains size measurements for 
penguins from three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, 
Antarctica.

The three species of penguins have quite distinct 
distributions of physical dimensions (@fig-penguins).

```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins
#| fig-cap: "Dimensions of penguins across three species."
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse, quietly = TRUE)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

title: Homework 4
text:
Questions Part 1

Question 1
In this problem, we will practice performing model diagnostics in a logistic regression model.
This question is taken from the Hosmer and Lemeshow textbook. The ICU study data set consists of a sample of 200 subjects who were part of a much larger study on survival of patients following admission to an adult intensive care unit (ICU). The dataset should be available in our shared folder. The major goal of this study was to develop a logistic regression model to predict the probability of survival to hospital discharge of these patients. In this question, the primary outcome variable is vital (survival) status at hospital discharge, STA. Clinicians associated with the study felt that a key determinant of survival was the patient’s age at admission, AGE. We will build to a multivariable logistic regression model while adjusting for cancer part of the present problem (CAN), CPR prior to ICU admission (CPR), infection probable at ICU admission (INF), and level of consciousness at ICU admission (LOC).
A code sheet for the variables to be considered is displayed in Table 1.5 below (from the Hosmer and Lemeshow textbook, pg. 23). We refer to this data set as the ICU data.
You will need to use some of the mutations implemented in HW 2, Q2, Part c.

We will use the following model: \[\text{logit}(\pi(\textbf{X}))=\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot I(CAN=\text{``Yes"}) + \beta_2 \cdot I(CPR=\text{``Yes"}) + \\ \beta_3 \cdot I(INF=\text{``Yes"})\]

icu = read_csv(here("data", "icu.csv"))
icu1 = icu %>% mutate(STA = as.factor(STA) %>% relevel(ref = "Lived"))
icu2 = icu1 %>% mutate(CAN = as.factor(CAN) %>% relevel(ref = "No"), 
                     CPR = as.factor(CPR) %>% relevel(ref = "No"), 
                     INF = as.factor(INF) %>% relevel(ref = "No"), 
                     LOC = as.factor(LOC) %>% 
                       relevel(ref = "No Coma or Deep Stupor"))


Part a
How many covariate patterns does the regression equation have?


Part b
Plot the standardized Deviance residual by predicted probability. Do you notice any potential outliers? Explain your reasoning.


Part c
Plot the Cook’s distance by predicted probability. Do you notice any potential influential points? Explain your reasoning.


Part d
Plot the change in predicted probability by predicted probability. Do you notice any influential points? Explain your reasoning.



Question 2
This question stems from an example from an online textbook by Dr. Ramzi W. Nahhas. The dataset for this problem includes a subset of individuals from the 2019 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH). Overall, our study aims included investigating potential risk factors for lifetime heroin use. Lifetime heroin use is a binary outcome, which we regress on age at first use of alcohol (alc_agefirst), age with 6 categories (demog_age_cat6), and sex assigned at birth (demog_sex).

load(here("data", "nsduh2019_adult_sub_rmph.RData"))
nsduh = nsduh_adult_sub %>% 
  dplyr::select(her_lifetime, alc_agefirst, demog_age_cat6, demog_sex) %>% 
  drop_na()


Part a
Using the nsduh dataset from the above chunk of code, please run a regression model using lifetime heroin use as our outcome, and age at first use of alcohol, categorical age, and sex assigned at birth as covariates in our model. No need to write out your model, you just need to write the R code to run the regression and display the summary.


Part b
Are we encountering a numerical problem with our regression? If yes, please name the numerical issue. What first clued you into that issue? Provide conclusive evidence of this numerical issue (with a contingency table), and explain which variable(s) are causing this problem.


Part c
What would you do to “fix” this numerical issue? Please apply your “fix” and rerun the regression



Question 3
In this problem, we will practice fitting and interpreting a log-binomial regression. 
This question is taken from the Hosmer and Lemeshow textbook. The ICU study data set consists of a sample of 200 subjects who were part of a much larger study on survival of patients following admission to an adult intensive care unit (ICU). The dataset should be available in our shared folder. The major goal of this study was to develop a logistic regression model to predict the probability of survival to hospital discharge of these patients. In this question, the primary outcome variable is vital (survival) status at hospital discharge, STA. Clinicians associated with the study felt that a key determinant of survival was the patient’s age at admission, AGE. We will build to a multivariable logistic regression model while adjusting for cancer part of the present problem (CAN), CPR prior to ICU admission (CPR), infection probable at ICU admission (INF), and level of consciousness at ICU admission (LOC).
A code sheet for the variables to be considered is displayed in Table 1.5 below (from the Hosmer and Lemeshow textbook, pg. 23). We refer to this data set as the ICU data.
You will need to use some of the mutations implemented in HW 2, Q2, Part d.


Part a
Write down the population equation for the log-binomial regression model of STA on AGE, CAN, CPR, and INF. How many parameters does this model contain?


Part b
Try using glm() to obtain the maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters of the log-binomial regression model in Part a. Do you run into any issues using glm()? If you try logbin(), does it fix the issues? Explain why and what warnings logbin() gives you.
Hint: keep the glm() function in its own code chunk so you can add #| eval: false. glm() may throw an error, so we want to show the work for glm() even though it’ll break your qmd rendering.


Part c
Using logbin(), obtain the maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters of the log-binomial regression model in Part a, but now take out age. Using these estimates, write down the equation with the fitted values.


Part c
Interpret the exponential of the coefficient (risk ratio) estimate for CPR.


Part e
We were not able to fit a model with age, but let’s just entertain a scenario here. Let’s say we fit the model in Part a and got a coefficient estimate of 0.29 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.23 to 0.35. Using the model is Part a, interpret the exponential of the coefficient (risk ratio) estimate for AGE.

title: Lab 1 Instructions
text:
Purpose
The purpose of this lab is to familiarize yourself with the Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey (WBNS) dataset, understand its structure and components, and prepare it for further data transformations. This includes downloading the data, organizing your project files, loading the data into R, and making initial modifications to ensure it’s in a working format for your project.

title: Lab 2 Instructions
text:
Purpose
The purpose of this lab is to prepare our data for further investigation using several data transformations. We will filter to our target subpopulation, select only the variables relevant to our project, and create new variables that combine information from multiple source columns. This is meant to take your practice on data transformation one step further: translating written human language to the needed action, function, and arguments.

title: Lab 2 Instructions
text:
2 Remove NA’s

2.1 Inverting a Deficit Variable into an Asset Lens
Many survey questions are framed around deficits (e.g., Q23 asks about eating less due to lack of money). To fulfill our asset-based goal, we will use case_when() to invert this into a positive framing. For example, a response of “No” to Q23 means a family maintained full dietary stability.






ImportantTask



Use mutate() and case_when() to transform your primary health/well-being outcome variable into an asset-framed factor variable. Use glimpse() to display your final, transformed data frame.

title: Functions
text:
What are functions?

R has many built-in functions that allow you to perform a variety of tasks
Functions usually take the form:


1function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )


1

function_name is the name of the function we are using.

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.

title: Functions
text:
Example: calling the seq() function

seq() is a function that generates a sequence of numbers.
It has three arguments: from, to, and by
Output will be the sequence numbers


seq(
1  from = 1,
2  to = 10,
3  by = 2
)


1

The argument from is assigned the value of 1, which is the starting point of the sequence.

2

The argument to is assigned the value of 10, which is the ending point of the sequence.

3

The argument by is assigned the value of 2, which specifies the increment between numbers in the sequence.




[1] 1 3 5 7 9

title: Functions
section: We don’t need to specify the argument names
text:
We don’t need to specify the argument names

We can run seq() without the argument names
R will assume that the values are in the correct order of the arguments

 
We get the same result:

seq(1, 10, 2)

[1] 1 3 5 7 9

title: Functions
text:
Output of a function

We can also assign the output of a function to an object using the assignment operator <-:


1function_output <- function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )                                     


1

The output of function_name is assigned to an object called function_output

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.





The output will not print, but it will be stored in the object function_output

title: Functions
text:
Now with the seq() function

We will assign the output of the seq() function to an object called odds:


odds <- seq(
  from = 1, 
  to = 10, 
  by = 2
)


So odds will now contain the sequence (1,3,5,7,9)

section: There are many ways to get help when you are stuck
text:
There are many ways to get help when you are stuck

Use the ? in front of the function name to get more information!

Usually if I need help with the arguments for a function

Google or go to stackoverflow.com

Often when I Google, I get redirected to something like stackoverflow
For example, let’s say my mean function was outputting NA. I would Google something like “keep getting NA for mean in R” Then end up here

I can also go to my favorite AI tool to get help

This is most useful for getting code started if it’s complicated (we’re not really at that level yet)
I asked ChatGPT “can you give me the code for calculating the mean in R”

This is what I got

For code generation, it gives you WAY too much
I also asked ChatGPT “Why is the mean function in R giving me an NA?” (in above link)

Ask another person!

This is the best way to get help, but also the most time consuming
If you ask a classmate, make sure you are asking about your code and not theirs
If you ask me, make sure you have a reproducible example (see below)}

text:
Quarto = .qmd file = Code + text
We can take .qmd files containing code (R and other types) + plain text (like we might make in Word), and then render to it other formats (html, pdf, Word, etc) that nicely display the code and text!

text:
Source File: hello.qmd
---
title: "Hello, Penguins"
format: html
execute:
  echo: false
---

## Meet the penguins

The `penguins` data contains size measurements for 
penguins from three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, 
Antarctica.

The three species of penguins have quite distinct 
distributions of physical dimensions (@fig-penguins).

```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins
#| fig-cap: "Dimensions of penguins across three species."
#| warning: false

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, palmerpenguins)

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan4")) +
  theme_minimal()
```

object_name <- value

Directly from the website:

Welcome to PUBH 523/623! This course provides an introduction to programming in R in public health, medicine, and related fields. Students will gain basic proficiency with the R environment and toolkit, focusing on reproducible workflows, data manipulation, visualization, and reporting. Topics include basic R programming, working in project-based folders, data transformations and summaries, data visualizations and plots, generating dynamic reports, and constructing summary tables. By the end of the course, students will be comfortable initiating data exploration projects in R and will be prepared to apply these skills in further analysis courses. No prior statistical or coding experience is expected or required.

title: Comments
text:
Describing your process with comments
Comments can be helpful for briefly describing what the following code does.

# Subtract 1 from 10, then divide by 2
(10 - 1) / 2

[1] 4.5

# Take the sine of 3
sin(3)

[1] 0.14112



Comment on every line is not necessary
As code gets more complex, comments can help you figure out your process

title: Comments
text:
Better use of comments

Use comments to explain the why of your code

 

Think of it as note-taking for your future self and others who might read your code

In theory, we should be able to figure out what we were doing
So we want to leave ourselves notes about why we were doing it, and any important details that might not be obvious from the code itself


 

For example:


# Calculate average age of 3 people
(29 + 42 + 68) / 3

[1] 46.33333

title: Functions
text:
R has many built-in functions that allow you to perform a variety of tasks
Functions usually take the form:


1function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )


1

function_name is the name of the function we are using.

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.

title: Functions

R has many built-in functions that allow you to perform a variety of tasks
Functions usually take the form:


1function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )


1

function_name is the name of the function we are using.

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.

title: Functions
text:
Example: simple function like mean()

mean() is a function that generates the calculated mean of a set of numbers
It has one main argument: x
Output (automatically printed) will be the mean of the numbers in x


mean(
1  x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
)


1

The argument x is assigned the value of a vector of numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)




[1] 3.5

title: Functions
text:
Example: calling the seq() function

seq() is a function that generates a sequence of numbers.
It has three arguments: from, to, and by
Output will be the sequence numbers


seq(
1  from = 1,
2  to = 10,
3  by = 2
)


1

The argument from is assigned the value of 1, which is the starting point of the sequence.

2

The argument to is assigned the value of 10, which is the ending point of the sequence.

3

The argument by is assigned the value of 2, which specifies the increment between numbers in the sequence.




[1] 1 3 5 7 9

title: Functions
section: We don’t need to specify the argument names
text:
We don’t need to specify the argument names

We can run seq() without the argument names
R will assume that the values are in the correct order of the arguments

 
We get the same result:

seq(1, 10, 2)

[1] 1 3 5 7 9

title: Functions
text:
Output of a function

We can also assign the output of a function to an object using the assignment operator <-:


1function_output <- function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )                                     


1

The output of function_name is assigned to an object called function_output

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.





The output will not print, but it will be stored in the object function_output

title: Functions
text:
Now with the seq() function

We will assign the output of the seq() function to an object called odds:


odds <- seq(
  from = 1, 
  to = 10, 
  by = 2
)


So odds will now contain the sequence (1,3,5,7,9)

title: Functions
text:
Help with functions

If you need a reminder of how to use a function, you can use the ? or ?? to access the help file for that function:


1?seq
2??read_sas


1

The ? will take you to the help file for the seq() function, which will show you the arguments and how to use it.

2

The ?? will search for any functions read_sas from your installed packages and show you a list of functions that match that search term. This is helpful when you don’t remember the package a function is in.




 

Certain functions will show you the arguments if you press Tab after typing the function name and parentheses


mean()
sd()

 

R will also help autofill the names of functions from your loaded packages:


m
s

title: Practice 1
text:
Practice Questions
For Questions 6–10, complete your work in an R script and submit the R script into Brightspace. Your R script should be titled LastName_FirstInitial_Practice_01.R
Please be sure to use comments to label each question and part. Each question below tells you what to do in the script. You can use AI to get you started if you’d like. Here’s a chat I had with Claude to make a template R script.






Note



Note that this is not a math or statistics class, so don’t worry about units or interpreting calculation results in a real-world context. I only care about whether you can use R to do the calculations and whether you can write meaningful comments about what you are doing. If a problem asks for an interpretation, I mean something more like translating your written code into human speak.



Question 6
In your R script, use R as a calculator to complete the following. Make sure each calculation has a comment above it describing what you are doing.

Part A
Calculate the following expression:
\[\frac{(15 + 9)^2}{3}\]


Part B
A public health researcher recorded blood pressure readings (in mmHg) from three patients: 118, 132, and 126. Calculate their average blood pressure.


Part C
Calculate the square root of 144.



Question 7
In your R script, use relational operators to answer the following.

Part A
Is 7 times 8 greater than or equal to 60? Write the R code and run it.


Part B
What does the TRUE or FALSE output from Part A tell you? Write your answer as a comment in the script.


Part C
Before running the code, predict what each of the following expressions will return (TRUE or FALSE). Write your prediction as a comment next to each line, then run them to check.
100 / 4 == 25
17 != 17
3^2 <= 8
(5 + 3) > (4 * 2)



Question 8
Answer the following questions about R Scripts as comments in your R script.

Part A
What is the difference between running code in the Console versus running it in an R Script? Why is using a script generally better for your work?


Part B
List two ways you can run a line of code from an R Script in RStudio (keyboard shortcuts count!).



Question 9
Multnomah County’s public health department tracks chlamydia cases across neighborhoods in Portland as part of routine STI surveillance. Chlamydia is the most commonly reported STI in Multnomah County, and monitoring its spread at the neighborhood level helps the health department decide where to direct testing and outreach resources.
A health analyst has written the following code to calculate the chlamydia case rate for a neighborhood cluster in Northeast Portland. The four numbers being added represent chlamydia case counts reported from four zip codes (97211, 97212, 97213, and 97218) in 2023. The population of 50,000 reflects the combined resident population across those zip codes. The rate is calculated per 10,000 residents — a common scaling choice in public health that makes rates easier to interpret and compare across areas of different sizes.
The code works correctly, but has no comments. In your R script, copy this code and add meaningful comments to explain what each line is doing and why it matters in this public health context. Do not change the code itself — only add comments.
total_cases <- 520 + 310 + 480 + 275

population <- 50000

rate_per_10k <- (total_cases / population) * 10000

rate_per_10k


Question 10
A county health department reports the following weekly flu case counts over 4 weeks: 42, 67, 55, and 38. In your R script, complete the following. Each calculation should have a comment explaining what you are doing.

Part A
Calculate the total number of flu cases across all 4 weeks.


Part B
Calculate the average weekly case count.


Part C
Use a relational operator to check whether the average weekly case count is greater than 50. Write a comment interpreting what the result tells you.

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
What’s in a name?
Object names must start with a letter and can only contain letters, numbers, _, and .. You want your object names to be descriptive, so you’ll need to adopt a convention for multiple words. We recommend snake_case, where you separate lowercase words with _.

i_use_snake_case
otherPeopleUseCamelCase
some.people.use.periods
And_aFew.People_RENOUNCEconvention

We’ll return to names again when we discuss code style in ?@sec-workflow-style.
You can inspect an object by typing its name:

x <- 3
x

[1] 3

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Make another assignment:

this_is_a_really_long_name <- 2.5

To inspect this object, try out RStudio’s completion facility: type “this”, press TAB, add characters until you have a unique prefix, then press return.
Let’s assume you made a mistake, and that the value of this_is_a_really_long_name should be 3.5, not 2.5. You can use another keyboard shortcut to help you fix it. For example, you can press ↑ to bring the last command you typed and edit it. Or, type “this” then press Cmd/Ctrl + ↑ to list all the commands you’ve typed that start with those letters. Use the arrow keys to navigate, then press enter to retype the command.

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Change 2.5 to 3.5 and rerun.
Make yet another assignment:

r_rocks <- 2^3

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Let’s try to inspect it:

r_rock
#> Error: object 'r_rock' not found
R_rocks
#> Error: object 'R_rocks' not found

This illustrates the implied contract between you and R: R will do the tedious computations for you, but in exchange, you must be completely precise in your instructions. If not, you’re likely to get an error that says the object you’re looking for was not found. Typos matter; R can’t read your mind and say, “oh, they probably meant r_rocks when they typed r_rock”. Case matters; similarly, R can’t read your mind and say, “oh, they probably meant r_rocks when they typed R_rocks”.

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Why does file organization matter?
Good organization means you can:

Find files without hunting
Re-run your analysis months later
Share your work without thorough explanations
Avoid broken paths and missing files
Collaborate without stepping on each other

title: Folder and file organization
text:
The Core Principle: Self-Contained Projects
Every analysis project should live in one folder that contains everything needed to reproduce it.

my_analysis/         ← Everything lives here
├── data/
├── scripts/
├── outputs/
└── README.md

If you moved this folder to another computer, it should still work.






Warning


Avoid scattering files across your Desktop, Downloads, and Documents. Future you will not remember where anything is.

title: Folder and file organization
text:
A Standard Folder Structure
my_project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/          # Original data — never modify this
│   └── processed/    # Cleaned, transformed data
├── scripts/          # Your R scripts
├── outputs/
│   ├── figures/      # Plots and charts
│   └── tables/       # Summary tables, exports
├── docs/             # Reports, notes, references
└── README.md         # What this project is and how to run it







Tip


You don’t need every folder for every project — but data/raw/, scripts/, and outputs/ are almost always worth having.

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Raw Data is Sacred


Never modify raw data files.
Treat data/raw/ as read-only:

Load it in R
Clean and transform in a script
Save results to data/processed/


# Good workflow
raw <- read.csv("data/raw/survey.csv")

cleaned <- raw |>
  filter(!is.na(age)) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(age, breaks = c(0, 30, 60, 100)))

write.csv(cleaned,
          "data/processed/survey_clean.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)


If you ever need to start over, your original data is untouched.

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Naming Files: The Rules


Avoid ❌
Final version.R
analysis REVISED.R
data (2).csv
my script v3 FINAL2.R
Script for Sarah.R
untitled.R

Prefer ✅
01_clean_data.R
02_exploratory_analysis.R
03_model_fitting.R
survey_responses_2024.csv
species_counts_raw.csv
README.md

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Naming Conventions: Three Rules
1. Use lowercase letters and underscores (or hyphens)
# Good
clean_data.R        survey-responses.csv

# Avoid
Clean Data.R        Survey Responses.csv    cleanData.R

2. Be descriptive, but concise
# Good           # Too vague    # Too long
03_model.R       script3.R      third_script_for_the_linear_model_analysis.R


3. Use numbers to indicate order
01_import_data.R
02_clean_data.R
03_visualize.R
04_model.R
This keeps files sorted correctly in any file browser.

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Naming Data Files
Include relevant context in the filename itself:
# Who / What / When / Version
participants_baseline_2024.csv
sensor_readings_site_A.csv
climate_monthly_1990_2023.csv







Tip


Dates in filenames: Use YYYY-MM-DD format (ISO 8601).
report_2024-03-15.pdf sorts correctly; report_15-03-24.pdf does not.





Avoid version-tracking in filenames:
# Avoid this — use version control (Git) instead
analysis_v1.R   analysis_v2_final.R   analysis_FINAL_forreal.R

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Absolute vs. Relative File Paths


Absolute path ❌
read.csv("/Users/jane/Desktop/
          my_project/data/raw/
          survey.csv")
Breaks on any other computer (or even after moving the folder).

Relative path ✅
read.csv("data/raw/survey.csv")
Works as long as you’re working from the project root.








Important


Rule of thumb: If a file path starts with / or C:\, it’s absolute and likely to break for anyone else.



We’ll cover R Projects and here::here() in the next lesson — they make relative paths easy and automatic.

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Organizing Your Scripts
Split your analysis into numbered, single-purpose scripts:



Script
Does




01_import_data.R
Loads raw data, minimal changes


02_clean_data.R
Filtering, recoding, joining


03_explore.R
Summary stats, exploratory plots


04_model.R
Statistical modeling


05_figures.R
Final publication-ready plots






Each script should be runnable on its own (given the right inputs exist), and should save its outputs to a known location
Files and output should only be dependent on files from earlier scripts in the sequence

# Survey Analysis — Spring 2024

Created a single top-level project folder

text:
Summary


The key habits:

One project = one folder — keep everything together
Protect raw data — never overwrite originals
Names: short, lowercase, no spaces — use _ to separate
Leading numbers for sequential files and folders
Dates as YYYY-MM-DD — for chronological order
Use relative paths — so code works anywhere





Good organization is a gift to your future self.
The five minutes you spend now saves hours of confusion later.

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Rule 1 & 2: Short, relevant, and lowercase
Keep names short and relevant — and use lowercase letters.

Too vague

script3.R
data.csv

Too long

third_script_for_linear_model_v2.R
all_the_survey_data_collected_2024.csv

Just right

03_wbns_modeling.R
wbns_data_2024.csv




Using uppercase is okay! This is something I do in our class documents. It’s just a little more annoying to type.

title: Folder and file organization
section: Rule 3: Use _ to separate words — no spaces!
text:
Rule 3: Use _ to separate words — no spaces!
Use underscores _ to separate parts of a name. Never use spaces.

Good

clean_data.R
clean-data.R
01_cleaning-data.qmd
survey_responses_2024.csv

Avoid

clean data.R
survey responses 2024.csv




Some people use hyphens - to separate words and underscores _ to separate larger sections — both are fine, just be consistent!

title: Folder and file organization
section: Rule 4: Leading numbers for sequential items
text:
Rule 4: Leading numbers for sequential items
Use leading numbers to keep files in the right order in any file browser.

01_import_data.R
02_clean_data.qmd
03_exploratory_analysis.qmd
04_model.qmd
05_figures.qmd




This works for folders too — great for organizing lessons, project phases, or any sequential workflow!
I also use something like z_misc to put a folder or file at the end of the order

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Rule 5: Dates in YYYY-MM-DD format
Including dates keeps files in chronological order automatically.

Sorts correctly

report_2026-01-15.pdf
report_2026-03-02.pdf
report_2026-11-20.pdf

Sorts incorrectly

report_15-01-24.pdf
report_02-03-24.pdf
report_20-11-24.pdf




Starting with the year means alphabetical order = chronological order.

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Rule 6: Versioning (optional)
You can label different versions of a file when you need to track changes.

analysis_v1.R
analysis_v2.R
report_draft_v1.qmd
report_draft_v2.qmd

 
Combine with dates for even more clarity:

report_2024-03-15_v1.qmd
report_2024-03-22_v2.qmd



Version labels are perfectly reasonable for coursework. For larger projects, clouds like OneDrive will save versions

title: Folder and file organization
text:
More on relevant naming

Relevant names are descriptive and help you remember what the file is for

 

To avoid issues between projects…

include the project name in the file name
include the info on what the file is/does in the file name
include the date in the file name
Some like 01_project-name_loading-data.R

title: R projects and working directories
text:
What is a Working Directory?
The working directory is the folder R is currently “looking at” — the starting point for all file paths in your session.
# See your current working directory
getwd()
#> [1] "/Users/jane/Documents/my_project"

# Any relative path starts from here
read.csv("data/raw/survey.csv")
# R looks for: /Users/jane/Documents/my_project/data/raw/survey.csv







Warning


If R can’t find a file, the working directory is almost always the culprit.

title: R projects and working directories
section: The Problem: Setting it Manually is Fragile
text:
The Problem: Setting it Manually is Fragile
You can set the working directory by hand — but you shouldn’t.
# Breaks on any other computer
setwd("/Users/jane/Desktop/my_project")

# Also breaks if you move the folder
setwd("C:/Users/jane/Documents/school/BIOL401/my_project")

This is exactly the absolute path problem from last lesson.
R Projects solve this automatically.

title: R projects and working directories
text:
What is an R Project?
An R Project is a file (.Rproj) that sits in your project folder and tells RStudio:

“This folder is the project root. Set the working directory here automatically.”


my_project/
├── my_project.Rproj   ← the R Project file
├── data/
├── scripts/
└── outputs/

When you open the .Rproj file, RStudio sets the working directory to that folder — every time, on any computer.

title: R projects and working directories
text:
Creating an R Project
In RStudio: File → New Project → New Directory → New Project


Give the project a name, choose where to save it, and click Create Project.
That’s it — RStudio drops a .Rproj file in the folder.






Tip


You can also create a project from an existing folder: File → New Project → Existing Directory

title: R projects and working directories
section: Opening and Using an R Project
text:
Opening and Using an R Project
Always open your project by clicking the .Rproj file, not by opening scripts directly.
# Once your project is open, this just works:
read.csv("data/raw/survey.csv")

# No setwd() needed. Ever.

RStudio shows the active project name in the top-right corner. If it says “Project: (None)”, you’re not in a project.






Warning


Opening a script directly (by double-clicking it) does not activate the project or set the working directory.

title: R projects and working directories
text:
The here Package (Bonus Tool)
For scripts in subfolders, use here::here() to build paths from the project root — even more robustly than relative paths alone.
library(here)

# Always starts from the project root, regardless of
# where the script lives
read.csv(here("data", "raw", "survey.csv"))
write.csv(cleaned, here("data", "processed", "survey_clean.csv"))







Tip


here() is especially useful in Quarto/R Markdown documents, where the working directory can behave unexpectedly.

title: R projects and working directories
text:
Summary


The workflow:

Create one R Project per analysis
Open work by clicking the .Rproj file
Use relative paths — no setwd(), ever
Optionally use here::here() for extra robustness


R Projects + good folder structure from last lesson = analysis that runs reliably anywhere, for anyone.


Up next: Reading data into R

title: Homework 2
text:
1 Purpose
This homework is designed to help you practice the following important skills and knowledge that we covered in Lessons 6-9:

Test a covariate for significance using the Wald test and LRT
Fit and interpret simple and multivariable logistic regression models
Interpret odds ratios and their confidence intervals
Evaluate model fit using likelihood-based methods
Apply data wrangling techniques to prepare variables for regression modeling
Communicate results of logistic regression analyses clearly and accurately in writing

title: Homework 2
text:
2 Directions

Please rename you homework as Lastname_Firstinitial_HW02.qmd. This will help organize the homeworks when the TAs grade them.

title: Homework 2
text:
3 Questions Part 1
The following questions are intended to give you practice in understanding concepts and completing calculations.

3.1 Question 1
This question is taken from the Hosmer and Lemeshow textbook. The ICU study data set consists of a sample of 200 subjects who were part of a much larger study on survival of patients following admission to an adult intensive care unit (ICU). The dataset should be available in our shared folder. The major goal of this study was to develop a logistic regression model to predict the probability of survival to hospital discharge of these patients. In this question, the primary outcome variable is vital (survival) status at hospital discharge, STA. Clinicians associated with the study felt that a key determinant of survival was the patient’s age at admission, AGE.
A code sheet for the variables to be considered is displayed in Table 1.5 below (from the Hosmer and Lemeshow textbook, pg. 23). We refer to this data set as the ICU data.


3.1.1 Part a
Write down the equation for the population logistic regression model of STA on AGE. What characteristic of the outcome variable, STA, leads us to consider the logistic regression model as opposed to the usual linear regression model to describe the relationship between STA and AGE?


3.1.2 Part b
Write down an expression for the log-likelihood for the logistic regression model in Part a. This will be a mathematical expression. Please do not use generic expressions like \(\pi(X)\), instead replace \(X\) with the specific variables in this question.


3.1.3 Part c
Using the glm() function, obtain the maximum likelihood estimates of the coefficient parameters of the logistic regression model in Part a. Using these estimates, write down the equation for the fitted logistic regression model.


3.1.4 Part d
Use the Wald test to test whether or not the intercept (\(\beta_0\)) of the logistic regression model is significantly different from 0. Make sure to follow the steps laid out in class and include: hypothesis test, code/work leading to the computed test statistic, output including the test statistic and p-value, and conclusion.


3.1.5 Part e
Use the Likelihood Ratio test to test whether or not the coefficient for age (\(\beta_1\)) of the logistic regression model is significantly different from 0. Make sure to follow the steps laid out in class and include: hypothesis test, code/work leading to the computed test statistic, output including the test statistic and p-value, and conclusion.


3.1.6 Part f
Write a sentence interpreting the estimated odds ratio for age (the coefficient in Part e). Please include the 95% confidence interval.


3.1.7 Part g
Write a sentence interpreting the estimated odds ratio for a 10-year increase in age. Please include the 95% confidence interval. (Hint: We’re scaling up the coefficient 10 times)


3.1.8 Part h
Compute the predicted probability of hospital discharge for a subject who is 63 years old. Compute the 95% confidence interval for the predicted probability and interpret the predicted probability.



3.2 Question 2
We will continue to work with the ICU data in Question 1. Please refer back to the information above. In this question, we will use the ICU data to fit a multivariable logistic regression model.

3.2.1 Part a
From the above list (AGE, CAN, CPR, INF, and LOC) of independent variables, identify if each is a continuous, binary, or multi-level (>2) categorical variable.


3.2.2 Part b
For the binary and multi-level categorical variables, please identify a reference group for each. Include justification for the reference group.


3.2.3 Part c
For the categorical variables (binary and multi-group), please mutate the variables within the ICU dataset to set your chosen reference groups.


3.2.4 Part d
Write down the equation for the logistic regression model of STA on CPR.


3.2.5 Part e
Using the glm() function, obtain the maximum likelihood estimates of the coefficient parameters of the logistic regression model in Part d (Section 3.2.4). Using these estimates, write down fitted logistic regression model.


3.2.6 Part f
Write a sentence interpreting the odds ratio for the CPR in Part e’s model. Please include the 95% confidence interval.


3.2.7 Part g
Write down the equation for the logistic regression model of STA on LOC.


3.2.8 Part h
Using the glm() function, obtain the maximum likelihood estimates of the coefficient parameters of the logistic regression model in Part h. Present the coefficient estimates. No need to write out the fitted regression equation.
Please take note of the warnings that you receive from fitting the glm() model and any large coefficient estimate with large confidence intervals. In this case, we have a category within LOC that has very few observations. (We will discuss this more in Lesson 14: Numerical Problems)
Check the number of observations that have a deep stupor and death at discharge and the number of observations that have a deep stupor and live at discharge. You can do this using the table() function to create a contingency table.


3.2.9 Part i
Write a sentence interpreting the odds ratio of death for the indicator of coma. Please include the 95% confidence interval.

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
What is Quarto?

Quarto is a publishing system that lets us combine text and code into a single document
It is the successor to R Markdown — you may see both names online, but we’ll use Quarto


Artwork by @allison_horst

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
A complete .qmd file
Here’s what a full .qmd file looks like — we’ll break down each piece next.
---
title: "Hello, Penguins"       
format: html                   
execute:
  echo: false
---

## Meet the penguins           

The `penguins` data contains size measurements for 
penguins from three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, 
Antarctica.

```{r}                        
#| label: fig-penguins
#| warning: false

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, palmerpenguins)

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
3 types of content in a .qmd
Every .qmd file is made up of exactly three things:

YAML metadata — settings at the top of the file (title, author, output format)
Text — plain writing, lists, images, links
Code chunks — blocks of R (or other) code

We’ll look at each one in detail — but first, let’s see them all together in a real example.

Illustration by Alison Hill and Allison Horst, for RStudio.

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
2. Text
Outside of code chunks, you write plain text using Markdown formatting:
## This is a heading

### This is a subheading

This is a regular paragraph. You can make text **bold** or *italic*.

- This is a bullet point
- Another bullet point

More R Markdown capabilities

rmarkdown Cheatsheet
In RStudio: Help → Markdown Quick Reference




Tip: Use the Visual Editor (top of the editor window) for a Word-like experience if you prefer not to write raw Markdown yet.

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
Code chunk options
You can control how a chunk behaves with #| options at the top of the chunk:



Option
What it does




echo: false
Hides the code in output (results still show)


warning: false
Hides warnings from the output


include: false
Hides both code and results (still runs)


eval: false
Don’t run the code (no output)



```{r}
1#| echo: false
#| warning: false 
2#| eval: false
```

1

This is helpful if you do not want to show your code

2

This is helpful if your qmd file has code that doesn’t work or takes a long time to run, but you still want to render the document

text:
1. YAML metadata

The YAML block sits at the very top of the file, between --- lines
It controls settings like title, author, and output format

More YAML options on Quarto website



What I put in our practice files:

subtitle: "PUBH 523/623"
author: "Your name here"
date-modified: "today"
format: 
  html:
    link-external-newwindow: true

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
What is Quarto?

Quarto is a publishing system that lets us combine text and code into a single document
It is the successor to R Markdown — you may see both names online, but we’ll use Quarto


Artwork by @allison_horst

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
.qmd file = code + text
A .qmd file holds two things together:

Code (R or other languages) — the same code you’d write in a script
Text (like you’d write in Word) — headings, explanations, formatting

When you render the file, Quarto combines them into a polished output: .html, .pdf, .docx, and more.

Artwork from “Hello, Quarto” keynote by Julia Lowndes and Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, presented at RStudio Conference 2022. Illustrated by Allison Horst.

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
3 types of content in a .qmd
Every .qmd file is made up of exactly three things:

YAML metadata — settings at the top of the file (title, author, output format)
Text — plain writing, lists, images, links
Code chunks — blocks of R (or other) code

We’ll look at each one in detail — but first, let’s see them all together in a real example.

Illustration by Alison Hill and Allison Horst, for RStudio.

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
A complete .qmd file
Here’s what a full .qmd file looks like — we’ll break down each piece next.
---
title: "Hello, Penguins"       
format: html                   
execute:
  echo: false
---

## Meet the penguins           

The `penguins` data contains size measurements for 
penguins from three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, 
Antarctica.

```{r}                        
#| label: fig-penguins
#| warning: false

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, palmerpenguins)

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
1. YAML metadata



The YAML block sits at the very top of the file, between --- lines
It controls settings like title, author, and output format
---
title: "Hello, Penguins"
format: html
execute:
  echo: false
---

## This is a heading

rmarkdown Cheatsheet

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
3. Code chunks
Code chunks are where your R code lives
```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins
#| warning: false

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species))
```

There are 3 options to insert a new code chunk:


Click the  button at the top of the editor
Keyboard shortcut: Command + Option + I (Mac) / Ctrl + Alt + I (PC)
Type out ```{r} to start and ``` to close

title: Quarto and .qmd’s
text:
Code chunk options
You can control how a chunk behaves with #| options at the top of the chunk:



Option
What it does




echo: false
Hides the code in output (results still show)


warning: false
Hides warnings from the output


include: false
Hides both code and results (still runs)


eval: false
Don’t run the code (no output)



```{r}
1#| echo: false
#| warning: false 
2#| eval: false
```

1

This is helpful if you do not want to show your code

2

This is helpful if your qmd file has code that doesn’t work or takes a long time to run, but you still want to render the document

What is a working directory?


Working directory


The working directory is the folder R is currently “looking at.” When you want to locate a file, it is the starting point for all file paths in your session.

title: R projects and working directories
section: The Problem: Setting it Manually is Fragile
text:
The Problem: Setting it Manually is Fragile
You can set the working directory by hand — but you shouldn’t.
# Breaks on any other computer
setwd("/Users/jane/Desktop/my_project")

# Also breaks if you move the folder
setwd("C:/Users/jane/Documents/school/BIOL401/my_project")

This is exactly the absolute path problem from last lesson.
R Projects solve this automatically.

title: R projects and working directories
text:
What is an R Project?


R Project


An R Project is a file (.Rproj) that sits in a folder and tells RStudio: “This is where I want my working directory to be set automatically.”






I can add an R Project to my PUBH_523_26Su folder. The R project will show up as PUBH_523_26Su.Rproj.






PUBH_523_26Su/ 
├── PUBH_523_26Su.Rproj
├── admin/
├── data_lessons/
├── data_practice/
├── data_project/
│   ├── data_raw/  
│   └── data_processed/    
├── lessons/
├── practice/
├── project/
└── README.txt




When you open the .Rproj file, RStudio sets the working directory to that folder — every time, on any computer.

title: R projects and working directories
text:
Creating an R Project
In RStudio: File → New Project → New Directory → New Project


Give the project a name, choose where to save it, and click Create Project.
That’s it — RStudio drops a .Rproj file in the folder.






Tip


You can also create a project from an existing folder: File → New Project → Existing Directory

title: R projects and working directories
section: Opening and using an R Project
text:
Opening and using an R Project

When working with files in an R Project, you want to open and work within the R project

 

You can open an R project two ways:

Click on the .Rproj file in your folder
Open RStudio and select the project from the top-right corner of the window


 

Once a project is open, we can work in our files and do not need to set a working directory manually

R Studio will automatically set the working directory to the project folder




Opening a script/qmd directly (by double-clicking it) does not activate the project or set the working directory

title: R projects and working directories
text:
The here Package (Bonus Tool)
For scripts in subfolders, use here::here() to build paths from the project root — even more robustly than relative paths alone.
library(here)

# Always starts from the project root, regardless of
# where the script lives
read.csv(here("data", "raw", "survey.csv"))
write.csv(cleaned, here("data", "processed", "survey_clean.csv"))







Tip


here() is especially useful in Quarto/R Markdown documents, where the working directory can behave unexpectedly.

title: R projects and working directories
text:
Summary


The workflow:

Create one R Project per analysis
Open work by clicking the .Rproj file or opening in R Studio
Use relative paths: no setwd(), ever
Use here() to make relative file paths


R Projects + here() + good folder structure
=
analysis that runs reliably anywhere, for anyone

text:
What’s in a name?
Object names must start with a letter and can only contain letters, numbers, _, and .. You want your object names to be descriptive, so you’ll need to adopt a convention for multiple words. We recommend snake_case, where you separate lowercase words with _.

i_use_snake_case
otherPeopleUseCamelCase
some.people.use.periods
And_aFew.People_RENOUNCEconvention

x <- 3

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Make another assignment:

this_is_a_really_long_name <- 2.5

To inspect this object, try out RStudio’s completion facility: type “this”, press TAB, add characters until you have a unique prefix, then press return.
Let’s assume you made a mistake, and that the value of this_is_a_really_long_name should be 3.5, not 2.5. You can use another keyboard shortcut to help you fix it. For example, you can press ↑ to bring the last command you typed and edit it. Or, type “this” then press Cmd/Ctrl + ↑ to list all the commands you’ve typed that start with those letters. Use the arrow keys to navigate, then press enter to retype the command.

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Change 2.5 to 3.5 and rerun.
Make yet another assignment:

r_rocks <- 2^3

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Let’s try to inspect it:

r_rock
#> Error: object 'r_rock' not found
R_rocks
#> Error: object 'R_rocks' not found

This illustrates the implied contract between you and R: R will do the tedious computations for you, but in exchange, you must be completely precise in your instructions. If not, you’re likely to get an error that says the object you’re looking for was not found. Typos matter; R can’t read your mind and say, “oh, they probably meant r_rocks when they typed r_rock”. Case matters; similarly, R can’t read your mind and say, “oh, they probably meant r_rocks when they typed R_rocks”.

title: Functions
text:
R has many built-in functions that allow you to perform a variety of tasks
Functions usually take the form:


1function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )


1

function_name is the name of the function we are using.

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.

title: Functions
text:
What are functions?

R has many built-in functions that allow you to perform a variety of tasks
Functions usually take the form:


1function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )


1

function_name is the name of the function we are using.

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.

title: Functions
text:
Example: simple function like mean()

mean() is a function that generates the calculated mean of a set of numbers
It has one main argument: x
Output (automatically printed) will be the mean of the numbers in x


mean(
1  x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
)


1

The argument x is assigned the value of a vector of numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)




[1] 3.5

title: Functions
text:
Example: calling the seq() function

seq() is a function that generates a sequence of numbers.
It has three arguments: from, to, and by
Output will be the sequence numbers


seq(
1  from = 1,
2  to = 10,
3  by = 2
)


1

The argument from is assigned the value of 1, which is the starting point of the sequence.

2

The argument to is assigned the value of 10, which is the ending point of the sequence.

3

The argument by is assigned the value of 2, which specifies the increment between numbers in the sequence.




[1] 1 3 5 7 9

title: Functions
section: We don’t need to specify the argument names
text:
We don’t need to specify the argument names

We can run seq() without the argument names
R will assume that the values are in the correct order of the arguments

 
We get the same result:

seq(1, 10, 2)

[1] 1 3 5 7 9

title: Functions
text:
Output of a function

We can also assign the output of a function to an object using the assignment operator <-:


1function_output <- function_name(
2  argument1 = input_value1,
  argument2 = input_value2,
  ...
  )                                     


1

The output of function_name is assigned to an object called function_output

2

Within the parentheses of the function, there are set arguments that we assign values to.





The output will not print, but it will be stored in the object function_output

title: Functions
text:
Now with the seq() function

We will assign the output of the seq() function to an object called odds:


odds <- seq(
  from = 1, 
  to = 10, 
  by = 2
)


So odds will now contain the sequence (1,3,5,7,9)

title: Functions
text:
Help with functions

If you need a reminder of how to use a function, you can use the ? or ?? to access the help file for that function:


1?seq
2??read_sas


1

The ? will take you to the help file for the seq() function, which will show you the arguments and how to use it.

2

The ?? will search for any functions read_sas from your installed packages and show you a list of functions that match that search term. This is helpful when you don’t remember the package a function is in.




 

Certain functions will show you the arguments if you press Tab after typing the function name and parentheses


mean()
sd()

 

R will also help autofill the names of functions from your loaded packages:


m
s

text:
Organizing your scripts/quarto docs
Split your analysis into numbered, single-purpose documents:



Script
Does




01_import_data.qmd
Loads raw data, minimal changes


02_clean_data.qmd
Filtering, recoding, joining


03_explore.qmd
Summary stats, exploratory plots


04_model.qmd
Statistical modeling

Final publication-ready plots






Each script should be runnable on its own (given the right inputs exist), and should save its outputs to a known location
Files and output should only be dependent on files from earlier scripts in the sequence

title: Folder and file organization
text:
Wrap-up


The key habits:

One project = one folder — keep everything together
Protect raw data — never overwrite originals
Names: short, lowercase, no spaces — use _ to separate
Leading numbers for sequential files and folders
Dates as YYYY-MM-DD — for chronological order





Good organization is a gift to your future self.
The five minutes you spend now saves hours of confusion later.

title: R projects and working directories
text:
The problem with working directories

You can set the working directory by hand, but you should NOT!
When you set a wd manually, it will break if you move the folder or if you are on a different computer


1setwd("/Users/jane/Desktop/my_project")

2setwd("C:/Users/jane/Documents/school/BIOL401/my_project")


1

Breaks on any other computer

2

Also breaks if you move the folder





When you use qmds, running code in the console and rendering result in two different working directories

Let’s walk through an example!




R projects and the here package can help fix both of these issues!

title: Getting help
section: There are many ways to get help when you are stuck
text:
There are many ways to get help when you are stuck

Use the ? in front of the function name to get more information!

Usually if I need help with the arguments for a function

Google or go to stackoverflow.com

Often when I Google, I get redirected to something like stackoverflow
For example, let’s say my mean function was outputting NA. I would Google something like “keep getting NA for mean in R” Then end up here

I can also go to my favorite AI tool to get help

This is most useful for getting code started if it’s complicated (we’re not really at that level yet)
I asked ChatGPT “can you give me the code for calculating the mean in R”

This is what I got

For code generation, it gives you WAY too much
I also asked ChatGPT “Why is the mean function in R giving me an NA?” (in above link)

Ask another person!

This is the best way to get help, but also the most time consuming
If you ask a classmate, make sure you are asking about your code and not theirs
If you ask me, make sure you have a reproducible example (see below)}

title: Getting help
text:
Main ways to get unstuck

Use the ? in front of the function name to get more information!

Best for: understanding function arguments and usage

Google or go to stackoverflow.com

Best for: specific errors and edge cases

I can also go to my favorite AI tool to get help

Best for: getting code started or explaining errors

Ask another person!

Best for: when all else fails

title: Getting help
text:
1. R Documentation with ?
Type ?function_name in the console to open the help page for any function.



1?mean
help(mean)


1

These two commands do the same thing




Every help page has the same structure:



Section
What it tells you




Description
What the function does


Usage
The function signature


Arguments
What inputs it takes


Value
What it returns


Examples
Copy-pasteable code






Pro tip: Jump straight to Examples


Scroll to the bottom of any help page — the Examples section is often the fastest way to understand how a function works.

1example(mean)


1

Run the examples directly






If ? doesn’t help, try searching across all installed packages:

1??mean


1

Broader search of the function mean()

title: Getting help
section: 1. Demo: using ? to solve a problem
text:
1. Demo: using ? to solve a problem


Scenario: You want to round the number 3.14159 to 2 decimal places. You know there’s a round() function, but you’re not sure how to use it.




Step 1: Pull up the help page

?round

Step 2: Read the Usage and Arguments sections

Arguments and Examples are very helpful sections!

round(x, digits = 0)

x — the number to round
digits — how many decimal places (default is 0!)


Step 3: Try it out

1round(3.14159)


1

Default: 0 decimal places




[1] 3



1round(3.14159, digits = 2)


1

Now set digits to 2




[1] 3.14

title: Getting help
text:
2. Google and Stack Overflow


Tips for a good search:

Always include “in R” or “R programming” in your query
Copy and paste the exact error message into Google
Add the function or package name if relevant

Example: Getting NA from mean()

Google: "mean function returning NA in R"

This leads to answers like this Stack Overflow thread, where you’d learn about na.rm = TRUE.

x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
mean(x)             # Returns NA

[1] NA

mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)  # Returns 2.333...

[1] 2.333333









Reading Stack Overflow answers



Check the accepted answer (green checkmark) first
Look at the vote count — highly upvoted answers are usually reliable
Read the comments too — they often clarify edge cases
Check the date — R and its packages change over time

title: Getting help
text:
2. Demo: Google and Stack Overflow
Scenario: You try to combine two pieces of text in R and get an unexpected error.


The problem:

"Hello" + "World"    # This seems reasonable... but fails!

Error in `"Hello" + "World"`:
! non-numeric argument to binary operator


Step 1: Copy the error message and search Google:

Error in "Hello" + "World" : non-numeric argument to binary operator in R

Step 2: A Stack Overflow result explains that + is for math — string combining uses paste() instead.

Step 3: Apply what you found

paste("Hello", "World")          # with a space

[1] "Hello World"

paste0("Hello", "World")         # no space

[1] "HelloWorld"








Search tip


The phrase “non-numeric argument to binary operator” is a very common R error. Googling the exact error message in quotes is often faster than describing it in your own words.

title: Getting help
text:
3️⃣ AI Tools (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.)
AI can be a useful coding assistant — but you need to use it wisely.


When AI helps most:

Explaining what an error message means
Getting starter code for something new
Understanding what a function does

Example prompts: > “Why is the mean function in R giving me an NA?”

“Can you explain what na.rm = TRUE does in R?”

See an example ChatGPT conversation →

Watch out for:

AI often gives you more code than you need — focus on extracting the piece that answers your question
AI can be confidently wrong — always test the code it gives you
AI may use functions or packages we haven’t covered — stick to tools from class notes







Course policy on AI


If you cannot trace code back to the class notes, do not use it in assignments. You should be able to explain every line of your submitted code. See the syllabus for details.

title: Getting help
text:
3️⃣ Demo: Using AI effectively
Scenario: You want to find the largest value in a vector but you have no idea what function to use.


A vague prompt (less useful): > “how do i get the biggest number”
AI may give you a long answer with many options and extra explanation you don’t need yet.
A better prompt: > “In R, I have a vector of numbers: c(4, 7, 2, 9, 1). What is the simplest function to find the maximum value?”
AI response will likely point you to max().

Step 2: Test it yourself — don’t just trust it!

scores <- c(4, 7, 2, 9, 1)
max(scores)

[1] 9


Step 3: Verify you understand it

?max    # check the docs to confirm what it does







AI gives you a starting point, not a final answer


Always run the code yourself and make sure you can explain what it does before using it in your work.

title: Getting help
text:
4️⃣ Writing a Minimal Reproducible Example
When asking for help — from a classmate, on Stack Overflow, or from AI — a reprex (reproducible example) makes it much easier for others to help you.
A good reprex has three parts:


📦 Packages
List every package you’re using

library(tidyverse)


📋 Data
Use a small built-in dataset, or dput() to share your own

# Use a built-in dataset
head(mtcars)

# Or share a snippet of yours
dput(head(my_data))


💥 The problem
The code that produces the error

mean(c("a", "b", "c"))

[1] NA









The reprex package


The reprex package formats your example for easy pasting into Stack Overflow or GitHub. We’ll keep it simple for now — just focus on making your example self-contained and minimal.

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
What’s in a name?
Object names must start with a letter and can only contain letters, numbers, _, and .. You want your object names to be descriptive, so you’ll need to adopt a convention for multiple words. We recommend snake_case, where you separate lowercase words with _.

i_use_snake_case
otherPeopleUseCamelCase
some.people.use.periods
And_aFew.People_RENOUNCEconvention

We’ll return to names again when we discuss code style in ?@sec-workflow-style.
You can inspect an object by typing its name:

x <- 3
x

[1] 3

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Make another assignment:

this_is_a_really_long_name <- 2.5

To inspect this object, try out RStudio’s completion facility: type “this”, press TAB, add characters until you have a unique prefix, then press return.
Let’s assume you made a mistake, and that the value of this_is_a_really_long_name should be 3.5, not 2.5. You can use another keyboard shortcut to help you fix it. For example, you can press ↑ to bring the last command you typed and edit it. Or, type “this” then press Cmd/Ctrl + ↑ to list all the commands you’ve typed that start with those letters. Use the arrow keys to navigate, then press enter to retype the command.

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Change 2.5 to 3.5 and rerun.
Make yet another assignment:

r_rocks <- 2^3

title: Workflow: Naming
text:
Let’s try to inspect it:

r_rock
#> Error: object 'r_rock' not found
R_rocks
#> Error: object 'R_rocks' not found

This illustrates the implied contract between you and R: R will do the tedious computations for you, but in exchange, you must be completely precise in your instructions. If not, you’re likely to get an error that says the object you’re looking for was not found. Typos matter; R can’t read your mind and say, “oh, they probably meant r_rocks when they typed r_rock”. Case matters; similarly, R can’t read your mind and say, “oh, they probably meant r_rocks when they typed R_rocks”.

text:
2. Package errors (1/2)
Function not found
could not find function "x"...
This usually means you typed the function name incorrectly, or forgot to install or load the package.



1clean_names(iris)


1

clean_names() is from janitor — if it’s not loaded, R can’t find it




Error in `clean_names()`:
! could not find function "clean_names"


✅ Fix:

1library(janitor)
clean_names(iris) |> names()


1

Load the package first, then call the function




[1] "sepal_length" "sepal_width"  "petal_length" "petal_width"  "species"     





Install once, load every session



install.packages("janitor") — run once, downloads to your computer
library(janitor) — run every session, makes it available in R

Think of it like: install = buy the book; library = open it.

title: Common errors
text:
2. Package errors (2/2)
Masked functions — when two packages have the same function name
Error in select(data, var) : unused argument (var)


This is a classic error! Both dplyr and MASS have a select() function. Whichever package was loaded last wins — and if MASS was loaded after dplyr, you’ll get the wrong select().

library(MASS)
library(dplyr)
1iris |> select(Species)


1

Which select() is this? Depends on load order!




✅ Fix — be explicit with package::function():

1iris |> dplyr::select(Species) |> head(3)


1

No ambiguity — always uses dplyr’s version




  Species
1  setosa
2  setosa
3  setosa





Other common masking conflicts:



Package A
Package B
Function




dplyr
MASS
select()


dplyr
plyr
summarise()


dplyr
stats
filter()





The conflicted package forces R to throw an error whenever a masked function is used — great for catching these silently wrong results.

title: Common errors
text:
3. Object errors


Object not found
object 'x' not found
This means R can’t find a variable you referenced. Common causes:

1my_summary


1

This object was never created — code above may not have run




Error:
! object 'my_summary' not found



1install.packages(dplyr)


1

Missing quotes — R looks for an object named dplyr, not the text “dplyr”




Error:
! object 'dplyr' not found


✅ Fix: install.packages("dplyr")

File not found
No such file or directory
This happens when R can’t locate a file you’re trying to read in — we’ll see it in action once we cover importing data. For now, if you run into it, check:

Spelling of the file name
Forward slashes / not backward \
Correct file extension (.csv, .xlsx, .rds)
That you’re working inside the right R Project, so your working directory is where you think it is (recall our lesson on R Projects & working directories!)

Subscript out of bounds
Error in 'x': subscript out of bounds
You tried to access an element that doesn’t exist — e.g., asking for the 10th element of a 5-element vector.

title: Common errors
text:
4. Function syntax errors
Wrong argument name



1mean(c(1, 2, NA), remove.na = TRUE)


1

remove.na is not a real argument — R silently ignores it, and NA propagates through




[1] NA


✅ Fix:

1mean(c(1, 2, NA), na.rm = TRUE)


1

The correct argument is na.rm




[1] 1.5





How to find the right argument names


Run ?function_name and read the Arguments section — it lists every accepted argument, what it expects, and its default value.

?mean





Notice this one didn’t throw an error at all — it just quietly gave you the wrong answer! Not every mistake is loud. This is why it pays to double-check your output, not just watch for red error text.

title: Common errors
text:
5. Logic errors
These don’t always produce an error — the code runs, but gives you the wrong answer!


if statement errors
Error in if
This usually means an if statement was applied to something that wasn’t TRUE or FALSE:

x <- c(1, 2, 3)
1if (x > 1) print("big")


1

x > 1 returns a vector of TRUE/FALSE values — if expects just one




Error in `if (x > 1) ...`:
! the condition has length > 1



Silent logic errors (no error message!)

10.1 + 0.2 == 0.3


1

You’d expect TRUE, but computers store decimals in binary, and 0.1 + 0.2 is actually stored as a number very slightly off from 0.3 — so the comparison quietly returns FALSE




[1] FALSE


✅ Fix — use all.equal() or a small tolerance instead of == when comparing decimals:

1isTRUE(all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))


1

all.equal() checks whether two numbers are “close enough,” rather than checking for exact equality




[1] TRUE




Logic errors are the sneakiest bugs. Always check your output — don’t just assume a comparison did what you meant it to.

title: Common errors
text:
6. Factor errors
Factors look like character strings, but they have fixed levels — adding new values creates NA!


Adding a value not in the levels:

age_cat <- factor(c("child", "adult", "elder"))
1age_cat[1] <- "infant"
age_cat


1

“infant” is not a defined level — NA is introduced




[1] <NA>  adult elder
Levels: adult child elder




This error message gives it away:
invalid factor level, NA generated
If you see it, you tried to add a value that wasn’t in the factor’s pre-defined levels.



✅ Fix — convert to character first, then back to factor:

age_cat <- factor(c("child", "adult", "elder"))
1age_cat <- as.character(age_cat)
age_cat[1] <- "infant"
2age_cat <- factor(age_cat)
levels(age_cat)


1

Convert to character so any value is accepted

2

Re-factor with all levels present




[1] "adult"  "elder"  "infant"


Unexpected alphabetical ordering:

survey <- data.frame(
  rating = factor(c("Agree", "Neutral", "Disagree")))
1levels(survey$rating)


1

Default is alphabetical — probably not what you want!




[1] "Agree"    "Disagree" "Neutral" 


✅ Fix with levels =:

survey$rating <- factor(survey$rating,
  levels = c("Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree"))
levels(survey$rating)

[1] "Disagree" "Neutral"  "Agree"

title: Common errors
text:
7. Plotting errors


Not enough colors for factor levels
Error: Insufficient values in manual scale. 
3 needed but only 2 provided.

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_histogram() +
1  scale_fill_manual(values = c("orange", "purple"))


1

iris has 3 species, but only 2 colors were provided




Error in `palette()`:
! Insufficient values in manual scale. 3 needed but only 2 provided.


✅ Fix — provide one color per level (check if NA became a factor level too!):

scale_fill_manual(values = c("orange", "purple", "green"))


Extra + at the end of a ggplot chain
Can't add x object

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) +
1  geom_histogram() +


1

Trailing + with nothing after it




Error in parse(text = input): <text>:3:0: unexpected end of input
1: ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) +
2:   geom_histogram() +
  ^


✅ Fix — delete the final +
Extra %>% or |> in a dplyr chain
Similarly, re-arranging piped steps and leaving a stray pipe at the end (or middle) will break your code:

iris |>
1  filter(Sepal.Length > 5) |>


1

Dangling pipe — R waits for the next step but there isn’t one




Error in parse(text = input): <text>:3:0: unexpected end of input
1: iris |>
2:   filter(Sepal.Length > 5) |>
  ^

title: Common errors
text:
8. R Markdown / Quarto errors


Wrong chunk option names
Error in options[[sprintf("fig.%s", i)]]
Check that your chunk options use the correct names:



❌ Wrong
✅ Correct




fig.width = 5
out.width = "5in"


fig.height = 3
out.height = "3in"



Duplicate chunk labels
Error: Duplicate chunk label 'my-plot'
Every code chunk label in your document must be unique. Labels also cannot contain spaces.
```{r}
1#| label: my-plot-1
```

1

Add a number or descriptor to make each label unique



YAML indentation errors
---
format: html
  toc: true   # ❌ wrong indentation
---
✅ Fix:
---
format: 
  html:
    toc: true   # ✅ correct nesting
---


Chunk runs in console but fails on render
This usually means your document is relying on objects created earlier in your R session that don’t exist when rendering. The render starts with a fresh environment.
Always use Session → Restart R → Render to catch these before submitting.

title: Common errors
text:
Wrap-up: A troubleshooting checklist
When your code gives an error, work through this list:











Step
What to do




Read
Read the error message — what function? What keyword?


Typos
Check spelling, capitalization, commas, and matching parentheses


Packages
Is the right package installed and loaded?


Objects
Does the variable exist? Run ls() to list everything in your environment


Arguments
Run ?function_name and check argument names and types








Even experienced programmers encounter errors constantly. Getting faster at reading error messages is one of the most valuable skills you will build in this course.

title: Piping
text:
What is piping?

Pipes (and piping) are used to pass the output of one function as input into another function
You can think of pipes as “then” statements



I want to find my keys, then start my car, then drive to work, then park my car.




Nested

4park(
3  drive(
2    start_car(
1      find("keys")
      ),
    to = "work"
    )
  )


1

Our first action is embedded the furthest into the nested functions

2

Then the output of “find keys” in the input of “start car” which is nested as well

3

We keep working our way out to “drive”

4

Then we finally park





Piped

1find("keys") |>
2  start_car() |>
3  drive(to = "work") |>
4  park()


1

First statement is the first thing we want to do

2

Output of “find keys” is inputted into “start car”

3

Then we drive to work

4

Then we park the car





Pipes tend to match our sequential thoughts better
