title: Piping
section: Two types of pipes you might see
text:
Two types of pipes you might see

Two types: |> vs %>%

%>% is the original pipe in R (requires magrittr package within tidyverse)
|> is a newer pipe (started in 2021 and does not require a package)

Both pipes are used to write code from left to right

by passing the result of one step into the next






Example using |>



hrs_data |> dim()

[1] 2728   32







Example using %>%



hrs_data %>% dim()

[1] 2728   32






You can use either! Our notes will use |> since it is generally where the field is headed.

title: Piping and working with objects
text:
Two pipes in R: |> vs %>%

Both pipes are used to write code from left to right

by passing the result of one step into the next.

title: Piping and working with objects
text:
Background

The newer base R pipe |> was introduced in 2021 with the release of R 4.1.0.
The original magrittr pipe %>%

comes from the {magrittr} package and
became popular through the {tidyverse}.




Using the base R pipe |> does not require loading the {tidyverse} package (which includes {magrittr}),

while using the magrittr pipe %>% does require {tidyverse}.

title: Piping and working with objects
text:
Similarities

They work the same when the left-hand side becomes the first argument of the next function.
Example:



Using |>

hrs_data |> dim()

[1] 2728   32



Using %>%

hrs_data %>% dim()

[1] 2728   32

title: Piping and working with objects
text:
Differences
When do |> and %>% behave differently?

title: Piping and working with objects
text:
Simple example



|> is stricter and expects an actual function call on the right


hrs_data |> dim()

[1] 2728   32



hrs_data |> dim

Error in dim: The pipe operator requires a function call as RHS (<input>:1:13)



yrbss_data |> dim() works, but yrbss_data |> dim does not:


With %>%, we can omit the () after the function name:

hrs_data %>% dim()

[1] 2728   32

hrs_data %>% dim

[1] 2728   32

title: Piping and working with objects
text:
Advanced example

Code below runs a linear regression model with dependent variable bmi and independent variable age.
Using %>%:

note that for the data argument a . is used as the placeholder for the dataset yrbss_data since it’s already being “fed into” the model.



hrs_data %>% lm(height ~ age_yr, data = .)


Call:
lm(formula = height ~ age_yr, data = .)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)       age_yr  
   1.778463    -0.001525  



Using |>:
Using a . as as a placeholder for the data does not work with the newer base R |>:


hrs_data |>  lm(height ~ age_yr, data = .)

Error:
! object '.' not found



Starting with R 4.3.0, we can use a placeholder but it’s an underscore_:


hrs_data |>  lm(height ~ age_yr, data = _)


Call:
lm(formula = height ~ age_yr, data = hrs_data)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)       age_yr  
   1.778463    -0.001525

title: Piping and working with objects
text:
More advanced examples
See Learn more tab above for resources with more examples.

title: Piping and working with objects
text:
For this workshop
We will use |> because

it is built into R,
requires no extra package, and
works well for most {tidyverse} code you will write as beginners

Our older workshops and many reference materials use %>%.

title: Piping
text:
Simple vs complicated input


Simple: when the receiving function only has one input argument, we can use:





1hrs_data |> dim()


1

Just the function name dim with parentheses.




[1] 2728   32




1hrs_data %>% dim()


1

Just the function name dim with parentheses.




[1] 2728   32



 


Complicated: when the receiving function has more input arguments, we need to specify where the piped input goes. We do this with a placeholder:




The placeholder for |> is _

1hrs_data |>
2  lm(height ~ age_yr, data = _)


1

We take the hrs_data and pipe it into a function

2

This function lm requires multiple inputs. height ~ age_yr is one input and hrs_data is the other. hrs_data is represented by _ since it is piped through.





The placeholder for %>% is .

1hrs_data %>%
2  lm(height ~ age_yr, data = .)


1

We take the hrs_data and pipe it into a function

2

This function lm requires multiple inputs. height ~ age_yr is one input and hrs_data is the other. hrs_data is represented by . since it is piped through.

title: Piping
text:
Notice the code styling

We can start a new line after every pipe (|>)

R reads this as an incomplete line and will continue to read



1hrs_data |>
2  lm(height ~ age_yr, data = _)


1

With the |> R will look to the next line for where hrs_data is inputted

2

Then we follow with our desired function







If you have many functions in a row, putting each on a new line makes your code easy to follow!


1hrs_data |>
2  select(height, age_yr) |>
3  lm(height ~ age_yr, data = _)


1

With the |> R will look to the next line for where hrs_data is inputted

2

Then I select certain columns of my dataset

3

Then I run that through the lm function






You can further style the functions to make their input readable


1hrs_data |>
2  select(
    height, 
    age_yr
    ) |>
3  lm(
    height ~ age_yr, 
    data = _
    )


1

With the |> R will look to the next line for where hrs_data is inputted

2

select is not styled to highlight the input

3

lm is now styled to highlight the input

title: Getting help
text:
A huge part of coding is learning to debug your own code and figure out what’s going wrong.


The good news is that there are many ways to get help. These are some good steps (in order):

Use the ? in front of the function name to get more information!

Google or go to stackoverflow.com

I can also go to my favorite AI tool to get help

Best for: getting code started or explaining errors

Ask another person!

Best for: when all else fails

Operation
In R

We are grouping this statement to make it easier to read

title: Key operators and functions
text:
Is something in something else?

The %in% operator is helpful when you want to check if one thing is in a list of other things
Let’s say I have a vector


1my_vector <- c("a", "b", "c", "d")


1

We create a vector with letters a-d





I want to ask: “Is”a” in my vector?”


2"a" %in% my_vector


2

I want to see if "a" is in the vector




[1] TRUE



3"m" %in% my_vector


3

Then I want to see if "n" is in the vector




[1] FALSE



4"m" %in% my_vector | "a" %in% my_vector


4

We can combine operators as well! I’m asking: “Is”m” in my vector or “a” in my vector?”




[1] TRUE



5"A" %in% my_vector


5

It is also case sensitive




[1] FALSE

title: Import and Export
text:
Importing data

We often need to work with a dataset in R

These data need to be brought into our environment so we can work with them!


 

We can import data from many file types, including .csv, .txt, .xlsx, .rds, .sas7bdat, and .dta

 

Once imported, R typically stores data as data frames (or tibbles) if using the {tidyverse} package

Usually use the term dataset to generally refer to either a data frame or tibble

title: Import and Export
text:
rio package

The rio package provides a single, universal import/export function that works across many file types
Instead of remembering which package and function to use, import() detects the file type automatically from the extension


1hrs_data_rds <- import(here("data", "hrs_data.rds"))
2hrs_data_xlsx <- import(here("data", "hrs_data.xlsx"))


1

This will automatically use read_rds to import the dataset

2

This will automatically use read_excel to import the dataset





Great for quickly reading in data without worrying about the right package

 


Note: this is a new package! You will need to install it!

title: Import and Export
text:
Clean names

Variable names in real datasets are often messy: spaces, capital letters, special characters
The clean_names() function from janitor standardizes all column names


names(hrs_data_rds)

 [1] "HHID"          "pn"            "id"            "BIRTHYR"      
 [5] "BIRTHMO"       "BIRTHDATE"     "proxy"         "coupled"      
 [9] "sex"           "age_mo"        "age_yr"        "ed"           
[13] "degree"        "race_original" "smoke_ever"    "smoke_now"    
[17] "drink"         "height"        "srh"           "act_vig"      
[21] "bp"            "diab"          "cancer"        "lung"         
[25] "hrt"           "strk"          "psych"         "sleep"        
[29] "arth"          "cond_count"    "cesd"          "income"       

hrs_data <- clean_names(hrs_data_rds)
names(hrs_data)

 [1] "hhid"          "pn"            "id"            "birthyr"      
 [5] "birthmo"       "birthdate"     "proxy"         "coupled"      
 [9] "sex"           "age_mo"        "age_yr"        "ed"           
[13] "degree"        "race_original" "smoke_ever"    "smoke_now"    
[17] "drink"         "height"        "srh"           "act_vig"      
[21] "bp"            "diab"          "cancer"        "lung"         
[25] "hrt"           "strk"          "psych"         "sleep"        
[29] "arth"          "cond_count"    "cesd"          "income"       



Spaces are converted to underscores: “Age (years)” to “age_yrs”
Upper case letters are converted to lower case: “BIRTHDATE” to “birthdate”

 

Consistent, clean names make coding easier and reduce errors

 

Can be piped directly after import:


hrs_data <- import(here("./data/hrs_data.rds")) |> clean_names()

title: Import and Export
text:
Note on different variable types

When data is imported, R assigns each column a variable type (also called a class)
Common types you’ll encounter:




Type
R class
Example




Numeric (continuous)
dbl, num
3.14, 72.5


Integer
int
1, 42


Character (text)
chr
"male", "Seattle"


Logical
lgl
TRUE, FALSE


Date
date
2003-04-21


Factor (categorical)
fct
"low", "med", "high"




R doesn’t always guess the type correctly — always check with glimpse() or str() after importing
Incorrect types (e.g., a numeric ID read as dbl) may need to be fixed before analysis

title: Import and Export
text:
Exporting data

After cleaning or modifying data, you may want to save it to a file
Use export() from rio to write data to any common format:


1export(hrs_data, here("data", "hrs_data_clean.rds"))
2export(hrs_data, here("data", "hrs_data_clean.csv"))
3export(hrs_data, here("data", "hrs_data_clean.xlsx"))


1

Save a .rds file in the data folder

2

Save a .csv file in the data folder

3

Save a .xlsx file in the data folder





Prefer .rds for saving R objects between sessions: it preserves variable types exactly
Use .csv or .xlsx when sharing data with others outside of R

title: Import and Export
text:
Wrap-up

Today we covered how to import and export data in R from a variety of file types

 

Key takeaways:

Use file-specific functions (read_csv(), read_excel(), etc.) or import() from rio for convenience
Always check variable types after importing with glimpse() or tibble()
Use clean_names() from janitor to standardize column names
Use export() or file-specific functions to save cleaned data

title: Lab 1
text:
Purpose
The purpose of this lab is to familiarize yourself with the Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey (WBNS) dataset, understand its structure and components, and prepare it for further data transformations. This includes downloading the data, organizing your project files, loading the data into R, and making initial modifications to ensure it’s in a working format for your project.

title: Lab 1
text:
1 Lab activities

1.1 Familiarize yourself with the Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey






ImportantTask



Answer the following questions using information on WBNS:

What is the motivation for this study?
How could an information sheet on components of the WBNS help change policy?
Why is it important to study basic needs?





1.2 File organization






ImportantTask



Display your working directory using the here package and here() function.
Insert an image of your folder organization with the .Rproj file in the correct place.




1.3 Access and download the data






ImportantTask



No task to report back on. Just make sure you have the data and read the User Guide!




1.4 Load the data and rename the dataset






ImportantTask



Load your downloaded data file into R. Rename the loaded object to a clean dataset name of your choice. (Make sure to show the code for this!)




1.5 Decide on your project question






ImportantTask



Write down your chosen project option number and question.




1.6 Getting data in working format






ImportantTask



Remove the parentheses with values that are in front of the category names. Verify that the parentheses are gone using glimpse().




1.7 Save data for processing with .Rda






ImportantTask



Include a screenshot showing the new .Rda file within your data folder.

text: Resources

title: Common errors
text:
Error vs. Warning vs. Message



Type
Meaning




Error
Code stopped; something went wrong


Warning
Code ran, but R is flagging something suspicious


Message
Informational; not a problem



 
Example of a warning:

log(-1)  

Warning in log(-1): NaNs produced


[1] NaN



In this case, the code ran, but R is warning you that the result is NaN (not a number) because the logarithm of a negative number is undefined

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
Types of common errors

Typo errors
Package errors
Object errors
Function syntax errors
Logic errors
Factor errors
Plotting errors
R Markdown / Quarto errors



We will go through each type with real error messages and how to fix them. Keep this slide as a reference!

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
1. Typo errors


Missing comma
Error: unexpected symbol in:
"  geom_histogram(stat = "identity")+
  tidyquant::geom_ma(n=7, size = 2, color = "red" lty"


If you see “unexpected symbol”, the first thing to check is a missing comma.


R is case-sensitive — Mean() and mean() are different things!

1Mean(c(1, 2, 3))


1

Capital M — R can’t find this function




Error in `Mean()`:
! could not find function "Mean"



Mismatched parentheses

1mean(c(1, 2, 3)


1

Missing closing ) — the console shows + waiting for more input




Error in parse(text = input): <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
1: mean(c(1, 2, 3)
   ^


Quick fixes:

Use Tab to autocomplete function names and avoid typos
Check that every ( has a closing )
Use RStudio’s bracket highlighting — click next to a ( and its match will highlight
Press Escape if the console gets stuck on +

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
2. Package errors (1/2)
Function not found
could not find function "x"...
This usually means you typed the function name incorrectly, or forgot to install or load the package.



1clean_names(iris)


1

clean_names() is from janitor — if it’s not loaded, R can’t find it




Error in `clean_names()`:
! could not find function "clean_names"


✅ Fix:

1library(janitor)
clean_names(iris) |> names()


1

Load the package first, then call the function




[1] "sepal_length" "sepal_width"  "petal_length" "petal_width"  "species"     





Install once, load every session



install.packages("janitor") — run once, downloads to your computer
library(janitor) — run every session, makes it available in R

Think of it like: install = buy the book; library = open it.

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
2. Package errors (2/2)
Masked functions — when two packages have the same function name
Error in select(data, var) : unused argument (var)


This is a classic error! Both dplyr and MASS have a select() function. Whichever package was loaded last wins — and if MASS was loaded after dplyr, you’ll get the wrong select().

library(MASS)
library(dplyr)
1iris |> select(Species)


1

Which select() is this? Depends on load order!




✅ Fix — be explicit with package::function():

1iris |> dplyr::select(Species) |> head(3)


1

No ambiguity — always uses dplyr’s version




  Species
1  setosa
2  setosa
3  setosa





Other common masking conflicts:



Package A
Package B
Function




dplyr
MASS
select()


dplyr
plyr
summarise()


dplyr
stats
filter()





The conflicted package forces R to throw an error whenever a masked function is used — great for catching these silently wrong results.

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
3. Object errors


Object not found
object 'x' not found
This means R can’t find a variable you referenced. Common causes:

1my_summary


1

This object was never created — code above may not have run




Error:
! object 'my_summary' not found



1install.packages(dplyr)


1

Missing quotes — R looks for an object named dplyr




Error:
! object 'dplyr' not found


✅ Fix: install.packages("dplyr")

File not found
No such file or directory

1read_csv("my data.csv")


1

Typo, wrong path, or file doesn’t exist yet




Check:

Spelling of the file name
Forward slashes / not backward \
Correct file extension (.csv, .xlsx, .rds)
That you are in the right R Project

Subscript out of bounds
Error in 'x': subscript out of bounds
You tried to access an element that doesn’t exist — e.g., asking for the 10th element of a 5-element vector.

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
4. Function syntax errors
Wrong or missing argument names


A very common mutate() mistake — forgetting to repeat the column name inside recode():

iris |>
1  mutate(Species = recode("setosa" ~ "S"))


1

recode() needs the column name as its first argument




Error in `mutate()`:
ℹ In argument: `Species = recode("setosa" ~ "S")`.
Caused by error in `UseMethod()`:
! no applicable method for 'recode' applied to an object of class "formula"


✅ Fix:

iris |>
  mutate(Species = recode(Species,
1                          "setosa" = "S")) |>
  count(Species)


1

Pass Species as the first argument, then OLD = NEW pairs




     Species  n
1          S 50
2 versicolor 50
3  virginica 50



Wrong argument name

1mean(c(1, 2, NA), remove.na = TRUE)


1

remove.na is not a real argument — R ignores it and NA propagates




[1] NA


✅ Fix:

1mean(c(1, 2, NA), na.rm = TRUE)


1

The correct argument is na.rm




[1] 1.5




How to find the right argument names


Run ?function_name and read the Arguments section — it lists every accepted argument and what it expects.

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
5. Logic errors
These don’t always produce an error — the code runs, but gives you the wrong answer!


if statement errors
Error in if
This usually means an if statement was applied to something that wasn’t TRUE or FALSE:

x <- c(1, 2, 3)
1if (x > 1) print("big")


1

x > 1 returns a vector — if expects a single TRUE/FALSE




Error in `if (x > 1) ...`:
! the condition has length > 1


✅ Fix — use any() or all():

1if (any(x > 1)) print("at least one is big")


1

any() collapses the vector to a single TRUE/FALSE




[1] "at least one is big"



Silent logic errors (no error message!)

ages <- c(23, 31, 40, 45, 28)
1mean(ages[ages = 30])


1

= should be == — this silently does something wrong!




[1] NA


✅ Fix:

1mean(ages[ages == 30])


1

== is “equal to”; = is assignment




[1] NaN




Logic errors are the sneakiest bugs. Always check intermediate results with print(), head(), or View() to confirm your data looks right at each step.

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
6. Factor errors
Factors look like character strings, but they have fixed levels — adding new values creates NA!


Adding a value not in the levels:

age_cat <- factor(c("child", "adult", "elder"))
1age_cat[1] <- "infant"
age_cat


1

“infant” is not a defined level — NA is introduced




[1] <NA>  adult elder
Levels: adult child elder




This error message gives it away:
invalid factor level, NA generated
If you see it, you tried to add a value that wasn’t in the factor’s pre-defined levels.



✅ Fix — convert to character first, then back to factor:

age_cat <- factor(c("child", "adult", "elder"))
1age_cat <- as.character(age_cat)

7. Plotting errors


Not enough colors for factor levels
Error: Insufficient values in manual scale. 
3 needed but only 2 provided.

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_histogram() +
1  scale_fill_manual(values = c("orange", "purple"))


1

iris has 3 species, but only 2 colors were provided




Error in `palette()`:
! Insufficient values in manual scale. 3 needed but only 2 provided.


✅ Fix — provide one color per level (check if NA became a factor level too!):

Extra + at the end of a ggplot chain
Can't add x object

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) +
1  geom_histogram() +


1

Trailing + with nothing after it




Error in parse(text = input): <text>:3:0: unexpected end of input
1: ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) +
2:   geom_histogram() +
  ^


✅ Fix — delete the final +
Extra %>% or |> in a dplyr chain
Similarly, re-arranging piped steps and leaving a stray pipe at the end (or middle) will break your code:

iris |>
1  filter(Sepal.Length > 5) |>


1

Dangling pipe — R waits for the next step but there isn’t one




Error in parse(text = input): <text>:3:0: unexpected end of input

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
Wrap-up: A troubleshooting checklist
When your code gives an error, work through this list:











Step
What to do




Read
Read the error message — what function? What keyword?


Typos
Check spelling, capitalization, commas, and matching parentheses


Packages
Is the right package installed and loaded? Any masking conflicts?


Objects
Does the variable exist? Run ls() to list everything in your environment


Arguments
Run ?function_name and check argument names and types


Restart
Session → Restart R → rerun from top


Google
Search the exact error message + “in R”


Ask
Make a reprex and ask a classmate, in office hours, or on Posit Community








Even experienced programmers encounter errors constantly. Getting faster at reading error messages is one of the most valuable skills you will build in this course.

title: Common errors for data transformations
text:
Typo errors: Incomplete commands



When the console is waiting for a new command, the prompt line begins with >

If the console prompt is +, then a previous command is incomplete
You can finish typing the command in the console window



Example:

> 3 + (2*6

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
1: 3 + (2*6
   ^



> 3 + (2*6
+ )

[1] 15

text:
Error Type 1: Typo Errors
The most common error — and the easiest to fix!


Misspelled function or variable name:

# Typo in function name
my_data <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 6:10)
sumamry(my_data)

Error in `sumamry()`:
! could not find function "sumamry"



# Typo in variable name
my_datta |> head()

Error:

Mismatched parentheses or brackets:

mean(c(1, 2, 3)

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
1: mean(c(1, 2, 3)
   ^








Quick Fixes



R is case-sensitive: Mean() ≠ mean()
Use RStudio’s auto-complete (Tab key) to avoid typos
Check that every ( has a matching )

1library(janitor)

Subscript out of bounds

This happens when you try to access an element of a vector, list, or data frame that doesn’t exist


1x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
2x[3:10]


1

x is a vector of length 5

2

I try to access the 3rd to 10th elements, but some of them don’t exist.




[1]  3  4  5 NA NA NA NA NA



There is no error, but R returns NA for the elements that don’t exist

title: Common errors
text:
Wrong argument name

This can happen if you misremember the argument name, or if you accidentally type it incorrectly




1mean(c(1, 2, NA), remove.na = TRUE)


1

remove.na is not a real argument: R silently ignores it, and NA propagates through




[1] NA




Notice this one didn’t throw an error! It just gave you the wrong answer! Not every mistake is loud.



Fix: use the correct argument name


2mean(c(1, 2, NA), na.rm = TRUE)


2

The correct argument is na.rm




[1] 1.5







How to find the right argument names


Run ?function_name and read the Arguments section — it lists every accepted argument, what it expects, and its default value.

?mean

title: Common errors
text:
Silent logic errors (no error message!)

10.1 + 0.2 == 0.3


1

You’d expect TRUE, but computers store decimals in binary, and 0.1 + 0.2 is actually stored as a number very slightly off from 0.3 — so the comparison quietly returns FALSE




[1] FALSE


✅ Fix — use all.equal() or a small tolerance instead of == when comparing decimals:

1all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)


1

all.equal() checks whether two numbers are “close enough,” rather than checking for exact equality




[1] TRUE




Logic errors are the sneakiest bugs. Always check your output — don’t just assume a comparison did what you meant it to.

title: Intro to data transformations and summarizations
text:
dplyr basics

dplyr is a package in the tidyverse that provides a set of functions for data manipulation and transformation

 

Each function in dplyr is like a verb that describes the action being performed on the data

 

Most functions within dplyr have similar input and output:

Input: a data frame (usually the first argument in the function)
Output: a data frame
Additional arguments: typically describe what columns (variables) to operate on

title: Intro to data transformations and summarizations
section: Example of a dplyr function: select()
text:
Example of a dplyr function: select()




I can use the select() function to select specific columns (age_yr and ed) from my data frame (hrs_data)






1hrs_data |>
2  select(
3    age_yr,
    ed
    )


1

The first argument is the data frame we want to operate on (in this case, hrs_data)

2

select is the function we are using on the data frame

3

age and ed are the columns (in the data frame) that we perform the select() function on






   age_yr ed
1      55 NA
2      56 12
3      55 NA
4      50 16
5      71 16
6      52 17
7      62 11
8      51 13
9      70 16
10     56 NA

title: Intro to data transformations and summarizations
text:
Types of dplyr functions
dplyr functions can be categorized into four groups based on what they operate on:

Rows: functions that operate on rows of a data frame

Examples: filter(), slice()
Under the Data Transformation lesson series

Columns: functions that operate on columns of a data frame

Examples: select(), mutate()
Under the Data Transformation lesson series

Groups: functions that operate on groups of rows in a data frame

Examples: group_by(), summarize()
Under the Data Summarization lesson series

Joins: functions that combine two data frames based on a common key

Examples: left_join(), inner_join()
Not covered in this class

title: Intro to data transformations and summarizations
text:
Resources

dplyr cheat sheet

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
Data transformations on rows

We defined dplyr functions as operations that use columns as arguments

This is still true for row transformations
We use columns to define the rows we want to keep, remove, or modify


 

There are many functions that can be used to transform rows

 



We will cover the most common ones here:

filter()
arrange()
distinct()







Please note that I reduced the columns in hrs_data to make the output easier to read. The functions work the same way with all columns.

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
filter(): quantitative data

filter() allows us to keep rows (aka subset our data) based on conditions we specify (in the columns)
We input our data frame as the first argument, and then we specify the conditions for filtering in the second argument
We can use the following comparison operators to specify our conditions:

>: greater than
<: less than
>=: greater than or equal to
<=: less than or equal to
==: equal to
!=: not equal to

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
Example: filtering age_yr

Let’s filter on a numeric variable, age_yr: all rows with age_yr values greater than 99

We will expect to return rows with age_yr values of 100 and above from hrs_data



1hrs_data |>
2  filter(
3    age_yr > 99
    )


1

The first argument is the data frame we want to operate on (in this case, hrs_data)

2

The second argument is the condition we want to apply to filter our data (in this case, age_yr > 99)

3

The condition is specified using a comparison operator (in this case, >) and the variable we want to filter on (in this case, age_yr)




          id age_yr ed cesd             degree  srh
1 559512_010    100 14    2 Associate's degree Good

title: Data transformation: Rows
section: Example: filtering age_yr, now only exact matches
text:
Example: filtering age_yr, now only exact matches

Let’s filter on a numeric variable, age_yr: all rows with age_yr values equal to 38

We will expect to return rows with age_yr values of 38 from hrs_data



hrs_data |> 
1  filter(age_yr == 38)


1

Notice the change in the operator!! We are now using ==.




          id age_yr ed cesd          degree       srh
1 557909_020     38 16    1 Master's degree      Fair
2 553815_020     38 NA    0            <NA> Excellent
3 551116_020     38 NA    0            <NA> Very Good

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
filter(): categorical data

For categorical variables, we can use the same comparison operators

But now we need to filter on specific categories (levels) of the variable

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
Example: filtering degree

degree is a categorical variable
For categorical variables, we can only use == or != to filter on exact matches
degree has the following possible values: NA, None, GED, High school diploma, Associate's degree, Bachelor's degree, and Master's degree, Professional degree (Ph.D./M.D./JD)


hrs_data |>
1  filter(degree == "Master's degree")

title: Data transformation: Rows
section: WAIT! Did those two operations have different rows?
text:
WAIT! Did those two operations have different rows?

It’s always good to check your output!

 

I did not notice that filter_out() and filter() with != had different outputs until I checked the number of rows in each output

 

filter_out() keeps the NA values, while filter() with != does not keep the NA values (because NA is not equal to anything, including itself)







When using !=, I suggest using filter_out()

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
Sorting datasets using arrange()

arrange() changes the order of the rows in a dataset based on the values in one or more columns

 

You can arrange by ascending or descending order

 

Why use arrange()?

Visual clarity when you look at data (see a variable ordered)
Helpful in conjunction with other functions (like count())

title: Data transformation: Rows
section: Example: sort data by ascending birth year
text:
Example: sort data by ascending birth year

By default, arrage_yr() sorts in ascending order:


hrs_data |> 
  arrange(age_yr)

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
distinct() keeps unique rows

distinct() allows us to keep only unique rows based on the values in one or more columns

 

distinct() can run without any arguments: it will return all unique rows in the dataset

This can be helpful if you want to perform a quality check on your dataset to see if there are any duplicate rows


 

distinct() can also take specific columns as arguments: it will return unique rows based on the values in those columns

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
Wrap-up

We learned three functions that allow us to transform rows in our dataset:

filter() (and filter_out())

Keep rows based on conditions we specify in the columns

arrange()

Sort rows based on the values in one or more columns

distinct()

Keep only unique rows based on the values in one or more columns

title: Data transformation: Rows
text:
filter()

filter() allows us to keep rows (aka subset our data) based on conditions we specify (in the columns)
We input our data frame as the first argument, and then we specify the conditions for filtering in the second argument




We can use the following comparison operators to specify our conditions:

>: greater than
<: less than
>=: greater than or equal to
<=: less than or equal to
==: equal to
!=: not equal to






Artwork by @allison_horst

text:
filter_out(): new companion to filter()

filter_out() requires {dplyr} 1.2.0 (or later version)
Allows us to filter out rows based on conditions we specify (in the columns)


hrs_data |>
1  filter_out(degree == "Master's degree")


1

We filter out anyone whose degree is a Master’s degree. This is the same as using filter(degree != "Master's degree") but it keeps the NA values in the output.

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
Data transformations on columns

We can use columns to create new variables, subset features, and reorganize a dataset
There are many functions that can be used to transform columns
We will cover the most column functions:

select()
relocate()
mutate()
rename()

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
mutate(): transform and create variables

mutate() allows us to transform existing columns and/or add new columns to the dataset

 

Think of this like adding a formula in Excel to calculate the value of a new column based on previous columns

 

mutate() is useful for:

Converting the units of one column to new units (e.g., months to years)
Performing arithmetic using multiple columns
Changing variable types or recoding categories

title: Data transformation: Columns
section: Example: calculating multiple columns and saving
text:
Example: calculating multiple columns and saving

We can create multiple new columns within a single mutate() function by separating them with a comma
Let’s save our work to a new object called hrs_data2 to avoid overwriting our original dataset


1hrs_data2 <- hrs_vars_subset |>
  mutate(
2    age_yrs = age_mo / 12,
3    age_decades = age_yrs / 10,
4    income_rounded = round(income, 0)
  )


1

We use the assignment operator <- to save the output into a brand new data frame called hrs_data2.

2

First, we create the age_yrs column.

3

Second, we create age_decades using the age_yrs variable we just defined in the step right above it!

4

Third, we create income_rounded by rounding the income variable to the nearest whole dollar.





Let’s take a look at the new data frame hrs_data2 to see our new columns

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
Subsetting columns using select()

The select() function allows us to isolate specific variables or columns from our dataset

 

Why use select()?

Drops unneeded information to maximize processing speed and visual clarity
Isolates specific blocks of data for focused modeling or visualization


 


Note: I will use select() in this lesson to make the output easier to read (with less columns)

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
Example: selecting specific columns

Let’s keep only the following columns from hrs_00: id, age_mo, income, diab, lung, drink, race_original, and sex

Column names do NOT need quotes in select()



hrs_01_vars_subset = hrs_00 |> 
1  select(id, age_mo, income, diab, lung, drink, race_original, sex)


1

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
Distinguishing filter() vs select()

Both filter() and select() are used to subset data, but they operate on different dimensions of the dataset

 

filter() is used to subset rows based on specific conditions

Think of this as filtering the dataset to keep only certain observations (e.g., only people who are 65+ years old)
We use this if we need a target population for analysis


 

select() is used to subset columns based on specific names or positions

Think of this as selecting only the variables we need for analysis (e.g., only the variables we need to calculate a new variable)
We use this if we want to reduce the number of variables in our dataset for clarity or speed

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
Renaming with rename()

You can rename columns with select() but it’s a bit easier to do this with the rename() function.
You just need to remember new_name = old_name ordering.
For example, I want to highlight to myself the limited representation in the race_original and sex variables

I’ll rename them to race_3 and sex_2 to indicate that they are limited to 3 and 2 categories, respectively



hrs_06_rename <- hrs_05_mutate |> 
  rename(
1    race_3 = race_original,
    sex_2 = sex
    )
names(hrs_06_rename)


1

The new name is on the left, and the old name is on the right.




 [1] "id"             "age_mo"         "diab"           "income"        
 [5] "lung"           "drink"          "race_3"         "sex_2"         
 [9] "age_yrs"        "age_decades"    "income_rounded"




If our variable names were something like “Age (years)”, we would need to write age_yrs = 'Age (years)' with single quotes around the old name because of the spaces and parentheses.

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
Reordering columns using relocate()

relocate() moves columns to a different horizontal position in your dataset
By default, variables sent into relocate() move directly to the very front of the dataset


1hrs_02_reloc <- hrs_01_vars_subset |> relocate(lung, sex)


1

Moves lung and sex to the very front of the dataset, before all other columns.

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
Wrap-up

We learned three functions that allow us to transform columns in our dataset:

relocate()

Reorder columns to a different spot in the dataset

select()

Subset specific columns to keep or drop

mutate()

Transform existing columns and/or create new columns

rename()

Rename columns with new names

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
relocate() + specify location

You can also specify where you want to move the column(s) using .before or .after arguments


1hrs_03_reloc <- hrs_01_vars_subset |> relocate(income, .after = id)
2hrs_04_reloc <- hrs_01_vars_subset |> relocate(income, .before = lung)


1

Moves income to place it directly after the id column.

2

Moves income to place it right before the `lung`` column.

title: Data transformation: Columns
section: Example: breaking code into multiple lines
text:
Example: breaking code into multiple lines

If code passes the vertical line in your editor pane, you can break it into multiple lines for readability




hrs_01_vars_subset = hrs_00 |> 
  select(id, age_mo, income, 
         diab, lung, drink, 
         race_original, sex)



hrs_01_vars_subset = hrs_00 |> 
  select(
    id, 
    age_mo, 
    income, 
    diab, 
    lung, 
    drink, 
    race_original, 
    sex
    )

title: Data transformation: Columns
text:
Example: calculating multiple columns

We can create multiple new columns within a single mutate() function by separating them with a comma


1hrs_05_mutate <- hrs_04_reloc |>
  mutate(
2    age_yrs = age_mo / 12,
3    age_decades = age_yrs / 10,
4    income_rounded = round(income, 0)
  )


1

We use the assignment operator <- to save the output into a brand new data frame called hrs_05_mutate. I’ve already used up to hrs_04_reloc in the previous examples.

2

First, we create the age_yrs column.

3

Second, we create age_decades using the age_yrs variable we just defined in the step right above it!

4

Third, we create income_rounded by rounding the income variable to the nearest whole dollar.

title: Data transformation: Columns
section: Some notes before we get into it
text:
Some notes before we get into it


Note 1: Assigning new objects


My code in this lesson is a mix of assigning new objects and not assigning new objects. I do not assign new objects show you the output of the function without extra steps.

For most of your work, you will want to assign your output to a new object.





Note 2: Naming conventions



I use hrs_00, hrs_01, etc. to indicate the order of my transformations
I use descriptive names for actions I take

Example: hrs_01_vars_subset indicates that this is the 1st saved object I make and the action I take is subsetting variables (columns)

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Filtering requires a little logic

We can chain multiple criteria using the & (AND) or | (OR) operators.

But we need to review a little logic before we do this.

If we wanted to return participants who identified as

Female and are in 10th grade,
we would use an & to chain these criteria together:


sex == "Female" & grade == "10th"

Note that SPELLING AND CASE MATTER!

You must write the name of the column exactly and
also the value (i.e. “Female” not “female”) exactly.

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Filtering with & (AND) criteria

This relational operator & is used to filter rows that meet both criteria
If we want to filter for participants who identify as diabetic AND have a Master’s degree, we would use:


hrs_data |>
  filter(diab == "Yes" & degree == "Master's degree")

Filtering with | (OR) criteria


This relational operator | is used to filter rows that meet either criteria


If we want to filter for participants who identify as diabetic OR have a Master’s degree, we would use:

  filter(diab == "Yes" | degree == "Master's degree")

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
replace_na()

Sometimes we want to fill in missing values with a certain value.
We can use the replace_na() function inside of mutate() to specify this.


Example 1Example 2Example 3



For example, suppose if the income variable is missing,

we want to replace it with the average income across the entire data set.



hrs_00 <- hrs_00 |>
  mutate(
    income_filled = replace_na(
      income,
      mean(income, na.rm = TRUE))
    )           

# check
hrs_00 |> 
  select(contains("income")) |> 
  tail()

We can also fill in missing values for character variables
Here we replace missingness in the female column with unknown:


class(hrs_00$female)
hrs_00 |> tabyl(female)

hrs_00 <- hrs_00 |>
    mutate(
      femalefilled = replace_na(female, "unknown"))

# check

title: Data transformation: Advanced
Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Select columns by data type

We can also select variables based on data types
where() is a helper function that returns columns where the inside function is TRUE,

We can use is.numeric, is.character, or is.factor to select columns of a certain data type



hrs_00 |> 
  select(where(is.factor)) |>
  names()

 [1] "hhid"          "pn"            "diab"          "degree"       
 [5] "proxy"         "coupled"       "sex"           "race_original"
 [9] "smoke_ever"    "smoke_now"     "drink"         "srh"          
[13] "act_vig"       "bp"            "cancer"        "lung"         
[17] "hrt"           "strk"          "psych"         "sleep"        
[21] "arth"          "income3cat"

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Example 1

hrs_00 |> tabyl(sex)

    sex    n   percent
 Female 1568 0.5747801
   Male 1160 0.4252199



Convert female to a new numeric variable called female whose values are

1 when female is Female, and
0 when female is Male


left side defines the condition ~ right side names the category

hrs_00 <- hrs_00 |>
  mutate(
    female = case_when(
      # when female is Female, make female equal to 1 
      female == "Female" ~ 1, # do not forget this comma!
      
      # when female is Male, make female equal to 0
      female == "Male" ~ 0
      )
    ) 

# checks
hrs_00 |> tabyl(female) # look at the categories
class(hrs_00$female)


How were the missing values (NA) handled?

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Example 2

Dichotomize the numeric variable income into two categories with 30 as the cutoff.

left side defines the condition ~ right side names the category

hrs_00 <- hrs_00 |>
  mutate(
    income30 = case_when(
      income < 30 ~ "<30", # don't forget a comma between cases
      income >= 30 ~ "30+"
      ) 
  ) 

# check
hrs_00 |> tabyl(income30)

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Example 3

Recode income to have 4 levels:

<20 (not including exactly 20)
20-30 (not including exactly 30)
30+
unknown if missing

Code comments

Notice that for the middle category we use an & statement similar to how we used logic in filter
New: used .default option to specify what to assign in all other unspecified cases.



hrs_00 <- hrs_00 |>
  mutate(
    income3cat = case_when(
      income < 20 ~ "<20",
      (income >=20) & (income < 30) ~ "20-30",
      income >= 30 ~ "30+",
      .default = "unknown"  # apply this in all other cases
      ),
    income3cat = factor(income3cat) # make it factor after creating categories
    )
  
# check
hrs_00 |> tabyl(income3cat)

Click here for a useful reference for all the different operators (both logical and comparison) that you can use.

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Data transformation: Advanced

We’ve covered the basics of transforming rows and columns
In this lesson, we’ll build on those skills with some more advanced techniques
We will cover:

Combining filtering conditions with logical operators (&, |, %in%)
Using arrange() after count()
Working with categorical data as factors
Creating variables with case_when()
Filling in missing values with replace_na()
Selecting columns with {tidyselect} helpers

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Filtering requires a little logic

We can chain multiple criteria using the & (AND) or | (OR) operators.

But we need to review a little logic before we do this.


 

If we wanted to return participants who identified as

Female and are in 10th grade,
we would use an & to chain these criteria together:



sex == "Female" & grade == "10th"

 

Note that SPELLING AND CASE MATTER!

You must write the name of the column exactly and
also the value (i.e. “Female” not “female”) exactly.

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Filtering with & (AND) criteria

This relational operator & is used to filter rows that meet both criteria

 

If we want to filter for participants who identify as diabetic AND have a Master’s degree, we would use:


hrs_data |>
  filter(diab == "Yes" & degree == "Master's degree")

 [1] hhid          pn            id            birthyr       birthmo      
 [6] birthdate     age_yr        ed            cesd          proxy        
[11] coupled       age_mo        degree        race_original sex          
[16] smoke_ever    smoke_now     drink         height        srh          
[21] act_vig       bp            diab          cancer        lung         
[26] hrt           strk          psych         sleep         arth         
[31] cond_count    income        income30      income3cat    income_filled
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)



Note that we could also use the comma in this case:


hrs_data |>
1  filter(diab == "Yes",
         degree == "Master's degree")


1

Comma is equivalent to “&” within filter()




 [1] hhid          pn            id            birthyr       birthmo      
 [6] birthdate     age_yr        ed            cesd          proxy        
[11] coupled       age_mo        degree        race_original sex          
[16] smoke_ever    smoke_now     drink         height        srh          
[21] act_vig       bp            diab          cancer        lung         
[26] hrt           strk          psych         sleep         arth         
[31] cond_count    income        income30      income3cat    income_filled
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Filtering with %in%

If we want to filter for multiple specific values in one column, we can use %in% instead of chaining several | conditions.
Example: if we wanted participants whose degree was “GED”, “High school diploma”, or “None”, we could use:


hrs_04_filter_degree = hrs_00 |>
1  filter(degree %in% c("GED", "High school diploma", "None"))
tibble(hrs_04_filter_degree)


1

%in% checks whether the value in degree matches any value in the vector we provide.

This is equivalent to, but much easier to read than:


hrs_00 |>
  filter(degree == "GED" | degree == "High school diploma" | degree == "None")



%in% is especially useful when you have many values to check within a single column

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Categorical data (factors)

IntroMake degree factorChange order of levelsBe careful!Replace degree with factor versionRemove extra variables



One data type that we haven’t yet looked at are factor variables

factors are how R represents levels of categorical data.

For the most part, you can use character and factors interchangeably for categorical data.
However, there are two main differences:

factors define the permissible values in a vector with an argument called levels.
The levels define the order in which the permissible values are displayed, such as in a table or figure.
The default order of levels (values) is in alphanumeric order.






Below we use the factor() function within a mutate() to transform degree from a character variable into a factor variable.


class(hrs_data$degree) # what's the data type of degree?

[1] "factor"

hrs_data |> tabyl(degree)

 degree    n percent valid_percent
    9th    0       0           NaN
   10th    0       0           NaN
   11th    0       0           NaN
   12th    0       0           NaN
   <NA> 2728       1            NA

hrs_data <- hrs_data |> 
  #create a factor variable
  mutate(degree_fac1 = factor(degree)) 

# Checks:
class(hrs_data$degree_fac1) # what's the data type of degree_fac1?

[1] "factor"

levels(hrs_data$degree_fac1) # what are its levels?

character(0)

# values are the same in the two degree variables:
hrs_data |> tabyl(degree, degree_fac1) |> adorn_title()

        degree_fac1
 degree         NA_
    9th           0
   10th           0
   11th           0
   12th           0
   <NA>        2728





Use the levels argument within the factor() function

Example: Create degree_fac2 variable as a factor version of degree with degrees in “correct” order:

hrs_data <- hrs_data |> 
  #create a factor variable
  mutate(degree_fac2 = factor(
    degree, 
    levels = c("9th","10th","11th","12th")
    ))

# Checks:
class(hrs_data$degree_fac2) # what's the data type of degree_fac1?

[1] "factor"

levels(hrs_data$degree_fac2) # what are its levels?

[1] "9th"  "10th" "11th" "12th"

hrs_data |> tabyl(degree_fac2)

 degree_fac2    n percent valid_percent
         9th    0       0           NaN
        10th    0       0           NaN
        11th    0       0           NaN
        12th    0       0           NaN
        <NA> 2728       1            NA

# values are the same in the two degree factor variables:
hrs_data |> tabyl(degree_fac1, degree_fac2) |> adorn_title()

             degree_fac2                    
 degree_fac1         9th 10th 11th 12th  NA_
        <NA>           0    0    0    0 2728





Recall that the levels of a factor are the permissible values in a factor.



Spelling matters!



If we try to use a factor level that doesn’t exist (“10” vs “10th”),

we won’t have any data in that category, and
the non-specified levels (“10”) get set to NA (missing).



hrs_data <- hrs_data |> 
  mutate(degree_fac3 = factor(
    degree, 
    levels = c("9th","10","11th","12th") # typo!!
    )) 

# check
levels(hrs_data$degree_fac3) # what are its levels?

[1] "9th"  "10"   "11th" "12th"

hrs_data |> tabyl(degree_fac3)

 degree_fac3    n percent valid_percent
         9th    0       0           NaN
          10    0       0           NaN
        11th    0       0           NaN
        12th    0       0           NaN
        <NA> 2728       1            NA

# compare
hrs_data |> tabyl(degree_fac2, degree_fac3) |> adorn_title()

             degree_fac3                  
 degree_fac2         9th 10 11th 12th  NA_
         9th           0  0    0    0    0
        10th           0  0    0    0    0
        11th           0  0    0    0    0
        12th           0  0    0    0    0
        <NA>           0  0    0    0 2728





Below we are doing something called reassignment:

We’re taking the previous values of our variable (degree),
doing something to them (making them a factor), and
then reassigning the variable degree to its new set of values.

I don’t recommend replacing a variable with new values until you are 100% positive that your code is correct!!

I can’t compare the new degree values to the original ones anymore to check my work



hrs_data <- hrs_data |> 
  mutate(degree = factor(
    degree, 
    levels = c("9th","10th","11th","12th")
    )) 

# compare to degree_fac2 (which we determined to be correct)
hrs_data |> tabyl(degree, degree_fac2) |> adorn_title()

        degree_fac2                    
 degree         9th 10th 11th 12th  NA_
    9th           0    0    0    0    0
   10th           0    0    0    0    0
   11th           0    0    0    0    0
   12th           0    0    0    0    0
   <NA>           0    0    0    0 2728

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
case_when()

IntroCodeExample 1Example 2Example 3



How can we dichotomize a continuous variable, such as income?
How can we combine categories of a variable, such as race?
How can we convert categories to numbers, such as female?

These are all examples where case_when() can be used.



The code follows a basic pattern for each category inside case_when():

condition ~ category name

The left side of the ~ is where we specify how to define the category.
The right side of the ~ is where we specify the category name.
Separate each “case” with a comma.




hrs_data |> tabyl(sex)

    sex    n   percent
 Female 1568 0.5747801
   Male 1160 0.4252199



Convert female to a new numeric variable called female whose values are

1 when female is Female, and
0 when female is Male


left side defines the condition ~ right side names the category

hrs_data <- hrs_data |>
  mutate(
    female = case_when(
      # when female is Female, make female equal to 1 
      female == "Female" ~ 1, # do not forget this comma!
      
      # when female is Male, make female equal to 0
      female == "Male" ~ 0
      )
    ) 

# checks
hrs_data |> tabyl(female) # look at the categories
class(hrs_data$female)


How were the missing values (NA) handled?





Dichotomize the numeric variable income into two categories with 30 as the cutoff.

left side defines the condition ~ right side names the category

hrs_data <- hrs_data |>
  mutate(
    income30 = case_when(
      income < 30 ~ "<30", # don't forget a comma between cases
      income >= 30 ~ "30+"
      ) 
  ) 

# check
hrs_data |> tabyl(income30)

      30+ 2647 0.97030792
      <30   81 0.02969208

[1] "character"

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
replace_na()

Sometimes we want to fill in missing values with a certain value.
We can use the replace_na() function inside of mutate() to specify this.


Example 1Example 2Example 3



For example, suppose if the income variable is missing,

we want to replace it with the average income across the entire data set.



hrs_data <- hrs_data |>
  mutate(
    income_filled = replace_na(
      income,
      mean(income, na.rm = TRUE))
    )           

# check
hrs_data |> 
  select(contains("income")) |> 
  tail()

title: Data transformation: Advanced
Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Select columns by data type

We can also select variables based on data types
For instance, select(where(is.numeric)) selects all numeric columns

(where() is a helper function that returns columns where the inside function is TRUE,
in this case is.numeric returns the TRUE/FALSE)



hrs_data |> 
  select(where(is.numeric)) |> 
  names()

 [1] "birthyr"       "birthmo"       "birthdate"     "age_yr"       
 [5] "ed"            "cesd"          "age_mo"        "height"       
 [9] "cond_count"    "income"        "income_filled"

hrs_data |> 
  select(where(is.character)) |> 
  names()

[1] "id"       "income30"

title: Data transformation: Advanced

Wrap-up

We learned several more advanced techniques for transforming rows and columns:

Combining conditions with &, |, and %in%
Checking your work with arrange() and count()
Working with factors
Create new variables based on conditions
Select columns by name pattern or data type

title: Data transformation: Advanced
section: Applying relational operators to filter rows
text:
Applying relational operators to filter rows

Recall the infographic from the previous lesson (Key operators and functions): 
We can use these logical operators to filter rows based on multiple criteria

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Example

If we wanted to return participants who identified as diabetic but DO NOT have a Master’s degree

We would use an & to chain these criteria together:



hrs_data |>
1  filter(diab == "Yes" & degree != "Master's degree")

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Filtering with & (AND) criteria (1/2)


This relational operator & is used to filter rows that meet both criteria


If we want to filter for participants who identify as diabetic AND have a Master’s degree, we would use:

hrs_02_filter_diab_MS = hrs_00 |>
  filter(diab == "Yes" & degree == "Master's degree")
tibble(hrs_02_filter_diab_MS)

More advanced data transformations

We’ve learned some important functions for transforming data for row-wise and column-wise operations:

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Replace degree with factor version

Below we are doing something called reassignment:

We’re taking the previous values of our variable (degree),
doing something to them (making them a factor), and
then reassigning the variable degree to its new set of values.

I don’t recommend replacing a variable with new values until you are 100% positive that your code is correct!!

I can’t compare the new degree values to the original ones anymore to check my work



hrs_00 <- hrs_00 |> 
  mutate(degree = factor(
    degree, 
    levels = c("9th","10th","11th","12th")
    )) 

# compare to degree_fac2 (which we determined to be correct)
hrs_00 |> tabyl(degree, degree_fac2) |> adorn_title()

names(hrs_00)

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
What are factors?

Factors are how R represents levels of categorical data

 

For the most part, you can use character and factors interchangeably for categorical data

Characters are just strings of text, while factors are a special data type that R uses to store categorical data


 

However, there are two main differences:

Factors define the permissible values in a vector with an argument called levels
The levels define the order in which the permissible values are displayed, such as in a table or figure
The default order of levels (values) is in alphanumeric order




Factors are the most useful data type for categorical data when you want to display your data!

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Code

The code follows a basic pattern for each category inside case_when():


hrs_00 <- hrs_00 |>
1  mutate(
2    new_variable = case_when(
3      condition1 ~ "category1",
      condition2 ~ "category2", 
      condition3 ~ "category3"
      )
    )


1

We are using mutate() to create a new variable called new_variable

2

We are using case_when() to define the conditions for each category of the new variable

3

Each condition is followed by a ~ and the name of the category that we want to assign to that condition. Each condition-category pair is separated by a comma.

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
What does case_when() do?

case_when() is a function that allows us to create new variables based on conditions

 

Examples of what we might want to do with case_when():

Categorize a continuous variable like income
Combine categories of a variable like degree
Convert categories to numeric

title: Data transformation: Advanced
section: Using case_when() to create a new variables
text:
Using case_when() to create a new variables

The code follows a basic pattern for each category inside case_when():


new_data_frame <- old_data_frame |>
1  mutate(
2    new_variable = case_when(
3      condition1 ~ "category1",
      condition2 ~ "category2", 
      condition3 ~ "category3"
      )
    )


1

We are using mutate() to create a new variable called new_variable

2

We are using case_when() to define the conditions for each category of the new variable

3

Each condition is followed by a ~ and the name of the category that we want to assign to that condition. Each condition-category pair is separated by a comma.

title: Data transformation: Advanced
text:
Categorize income into levels

Categorize the numeric variable income into two categories with $30,000 as the cutoff


hrs_05_income_fct <- hrs_00 |>
  mutate(
1    income30 = case_when(
2      income < 30000 ~ "<$30,000",
3      income >= 30000 ~ "$30,000+"
      ) 
  ) 


1

We are using case_when() to create a new variable called income30

2

If income is less than $30,000, we assign the category “<$30,000” to income30

3

If income is greater than or equal to $30,000, we assign the category “$30,000+” to income30





We can check the result by counting the number of participants in each category:


hrs_05_income_fct |> count(income30)

  income30    n
1 $30,000+ 1771
2 <$30,000  957

title: Data Summarization: Intro
text:
Data Summarization

There are many ways to summarize data in R

Each function can be useful in different scenarios!


 

We may need different tools based on the type of measurement (categorical vs. numeric)

Categorical data (represented as factors in R) will focus on frequencies and counts
Numeric data (represented as numbers in R) will focus on summary metrics like mean, median, standard deviation, etc.

title: Data Summarization: Intro
text:
Types of dplyr functions
dplyr functions can be categorized into four groups based on what they operate on:

rows: functions that operate on rows of a data frame (e.g., filter(), slice())
columns: functions that operate on columns of a data frame (e.g., select(), mutate())
groups: functions that operate on groups of rows in a data frame (e.g., group_by(), summarize())
joins: functions that combine two data frames based on a common key (e.g., left_join(), inner_join())

Not covering in this class (You can take BSTA 526 to learn about joins)

title: Data Summarization: Quick summaries
text:
Quick summaries

A good first step when working with data is to explore the dataset, variables, and observations

Does every variable have the expected number of observations?
Are there any missing values?
Are there any weird values that don’t make sense?

We want to quickly browse the data and get summary statistics for each variable

 

There are a few functions in R that give you automatic summaries of your data:

summary() in base R
skim() in skimr
get_summary_stats() in rstatix

title: Data Summarization: Intro
text:
Data Summarization

There are many ways to summarize data in R
We will need different tools based on the type of measurement (categorical vs. numeric)
Categorical data (represented as factors in R) will focus on frequencies
Numeric data (represented as numbers in R) will focus on summary metrics like mean, median, standard deviation, etc.

title: Data Summarization: Quick summaries
text:
Quick summaries

A good first step when working with data is to explore the dataset, variables, and observations

Does every variable have the expected number of observations?
Are there any missing values?
Are there any weird values that don’t make sense?

We want to quickly browse the data and get summary statistics for each variable

 

There are a few functions in R that give you automatic summaries of your data:

summary() in base R
skim() in skimr
get_summary_stats() in rstatix

text:
get_summary_stats() in rstatix

Only works for numeric variables — categorical variables are silently dropped
Flexible function: you can request just the statistics you want with type = (options include "common", "full", "mean_sd", "mean_ci", "median_iqr", and more — see ?get_summary_stats)

title: Data Summarization: Quick summaries
text:
Which one should I use?








Function
Best for
Watch out for




summary()
-A fast, no-setup check of a small dataset
-No standard deviation
-Output can be hard to read for many columns


skim()
-A first, fairly thorough look at a whole dataset (categorical + numeric)
-Requires skimr
-Output isn’t a plain data frame


get_summary_stats()
-Numeric summaries you want to reuse (e.g., in a table or plot)
-Grouped summaries (to be covered later)
-Requires rstatix
-Numeric variables only



 

In practice, you’ll often start with skim() to explore
Then use get_summary_stats() if you have certain numeric variables and statistics you actually need

Returns a data frame (a tibble), which makes it easy to use the results in further code, tables, or plots — this is its biggest advantage over summary() and skim()

title: Data Summarization: Grouped summaries
text:
Grouped summaries

Sometimes we want to compare summary statistics for different groups of people in our dataset
You can use group_by() to specify the grouping variable(s) before summarizing
Then you can use another summary function to calculate the statistics for each group separately
We will review the functions that can be used for grouped summaries:

summarise() from dplyr
skim() from skimr
get_summary_stats() from rstatix
tbl_summary() from gtsummary

Slightly different: does not use group_by()



 

For each, we will look at grouped summaries for:

Grouped by sex
Summarize age_yr, cesd, and income

title: Data Summarization: Grouped summaries
section: Two main functions for flexible summaries of numeric data
text:
Two main functions for flexible summaries of numeric data

get_summary_stats() in rstatix and summarise() in dplyr
When do we use one or the other?

get_summary_stats():

Quick and easy to use
Can be used for grouped summaries

summarise():

More flexible, but requires more coding
Can be used for grouped summaries

title: Data Summarization: Grouped summaries
text:
summarise() in dplyr

Unlike get_summary_stats(), you have to write out each statistic and name each resulting column yourself
This extra work pays off in flexibility: you can combine any functions you want (not just the built-in options), and you control the column names in the output
Add a group_by() before summarise() to get one row of statistics per group, just like with get_summary_stats()


hrs_00 |>
  summarise(
    mean_age = mean(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_age = median(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_age = sd(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_age = min(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_age = max(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Data Summarization: Grouped summaries
text:
Turning counts into proportions

count() gives you raw counts, but you’ll often want proportions or percents too
Use mutate() to divide the counts column (n) by its own sum

If the data are grouped (as below, by sex), the proportions are calculated within each group, since count() counts within sex but doesn’t remove the sex grouping until after

  group_by(sex) |>
  count(degree) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

title: Data Summarization: Tables
text:
tabyl()

tabyl() builds a frequency table for a categorical variable in one step, and returns three columns:

n: the count in each category
percent: that count as a proportion of all rows (including missing values)
valid_percent: that count as a proportion of only the non-missing rows

title: Data Summarization: Tables
section: Dressing up a tabyl() with adorn_*()
text:
Dressing up a tabyl() with adorn_*()

adorn_*() functions let you format that table for presentation
These are designed to be piped together, one after another








Function
What it does




adorn_totals()
Adds a total row and/or column (where = "row", "col", or "both")


adorn_percentages()
Converts counts to proportions (denominator = "row", "col", or "all")


adorn_pct_formatting()
Converts proportions to nicely formatted percents (control decimals with digits =)


adorn_ns()
Adds the raw counts back onto a table of percents, e.g. "45.2% (120)"

title: Data Summarization: Tables
text:
tbl_summary()

tbl_summary() builds a publication-ready summary table for all the columns you give it in a single command
It automatically picks sensible statistics based on each variable’s type:

Numeric variables: median (interquartile range)
Categorical variables: count (percent)
Missing values are shown as their own “Unknown” row

This is why we select() away ID/date columns first — tbl_summary() will otherwise try to summarize every column you give it

title: Data Summarization: Tables
text:
Customizing tbl_summary()

statistic = lets you change which statistics are shown, using { } to insert stat names like {mean}, {sd}, {median}, {n}, {p} (percent)
label = lets you rename variables to something more readable


hrs_00 |>
  select(age_yr, sex, diab) |>
  tbl_summary(
1    statistic = age_yr ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
2    label = age_yr ~ "Age (years)"
  )

Show mean (sd) for age_yr instead of the default median (IQR)

Introduction to ggplot2





Artwork by @allison_horst






Artwork by @allison_horst

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
ggplot2 in tidyverse





ggplot2 is tidyverse’s data visualization package

This is one of the main ways to create plots and explore data


 

The gg in “ggplot2” stands for Grammar of Graphics

 

It is inspired by the book Grammar of Graphics by Leland Wilkinson

Make graphs/plots by combining independent components
Start with a basic plot then add layers

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Works best with “tidy” data1






Each variable must have its own column.
Each observation must have its own row.
Each value must have its own cell.

Source: R for Data Science. Grolemund and Wickham.

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Grammar of ggplot2









ggplot2 needs at least the following three to produce a chart:

data, a mapping, and a layer


 

For the most part, there are default settings for the other parts:

scales, facets, coordinates, and themes

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Data

ggplot2 uses data to construct a plot
Works best with tidy data (when every observation is a row and each variable is a column)
First step in plotting:

Pass the data to the ggplot function, which stores the data to be used later by other parts of the plotting system

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Data

For example, if we intend to make a graphic about the hrs_data dataset, we would start as follows:


We input the data that contains our variables of interest.

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Mapping

Mappings use the aes() function to map variables to the different axes on a plot

aes() stands for “aesthetics”

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Data + Mapping

If we want the age and income columns to map to the x- and y-coordinates in the plot, we can do that as follows:


We use the aes() function to specify the mapping of variables to axes. In this case, we are mapping age to the x-axis and income to the y-axis.

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Layers

Every layer consists of three important parts:

The geometry that determines how data are displayed, such as points, lines, or rectangles
The statistical transformation that may compute new variables from the data and affect what of the data is displayed.
The position adjustment that primarily determines where a piece of data is being displayed

A layer can be constructed using the geom_*() and stat_*() functions

These functions often determine one of the three parts of a layer, while the other two can still be specified.

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Data + Mapping + Layers
Here is how we can use two layers to display the age and income columns of the hrs_data dataset as points and stack a trend line on top:

To create a scatterplot
To fit and overlay a line

We name the input argument for the dataset as data
We name the input argument for the mapping as mapping


More concise, no naming input arguments

Removed input argument name

We use the pipe operator to pass the dataset into ggplot()

section: We can also make plots with a single variable
text:
We can also make plots with a single variable

Data: still hrs_data
Mapping: using aesthetic to specify only one variable in the x-axis (age)
Layers: using geom_histogram() to show a plot of the counts per age


We specify only one variable in the aes() function, which will be mapped to the x-axis by default
We use geom_histogram() to create a histogram of the counts per `age

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
section: We can add more to plots!
text:
We can add more to plots!
We can change labels!

We use the labs() function to change the labels of the axes and title of the plot
We change the x-axis label to “Age (years)”
We change the y-axis label to “Frequency”
We change the title of the plot to “Distribution of Age”

Adding more to plots!
Increase (or decrease) text size so we can read it / it fits nicely!

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Notice: common components of ggplot2



Common components of ggplot2 include:

ggplot(): the main function to create a plot
aes(): the function to specify the mapping of variables to axes
geom_*() or stat_*(): functions to add layers to the plot
labs(): the function to change labels of axes and title
theme(): the function to adjust non-data plot elements such as text size,

title: Data visualization: Introduction to ggplot2
text:
Wrap-up

ggplot2 is great data visualization tool in R

 

Grammar of Graphics: data, mapping, layers, scales, facets, coordinates, themes

We can add a lot of different components to our plots to make them more informative and visually appealing


 

We discussed some of the options in ggplot2 but there are many more to explore!

Another online resource for data visualization with ggplot2: https://socviz.co/index.html#preface

What does summary() do?

summary() will show:

For categorical data: the counts in each category
For numeric data: the minimum, 1st quartile, median, mean, 3rd quartile, maximum, and count for NA’s


 



No package needed: it’s built into base R, so it always worksks
Downside: no standard deviation, and the output is harder to read/scroll through for datasets with many columns
Often what I use when I’m feeling super lazy, but not the best for a first look at a whole dataset

text:
What does get_summary_stats() do?

get_summary_stats() will show a table of summary statistics for each numeric variable

 



Only works for numeric variables: categorical variables are silently dropped
Returns a data frame (a tibble), which makes it easy to use the results in further code, tables, or plots: this is its biggest advantage over summary() and skim()

title: Data Summarization: Grouped summaries
text:
New summary function: summarise()/summarize()

Not necessarily grouped
Flexible function that allows you to calculate any summary statistic you want, and name the resulting columns yourself

You need to feed it a column and a function to apply to that column


 



Really flexible: you can calculate custom summary statistics
More work if you want general summary statistics: you have to write out each statistic and name each resulting column yourself

title: Data Summarization: Grouped summaries
text:
Example: summary statistics on age

For each summary statistic, I need to use the designated function and specify the column I want to summarize


hrs_00 |>
  summarise(
    mean_age = mean(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE),
1    mean_age_above_80 = mean(age_yr[age_yr > 80], na.rm = TRUE),
    median_age = median(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_age = sd(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_age = min(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_age = max(age_yr, na.rm = TRUE), 
  )


1

I can create a unique summary statistic without changing the dataset. I have calculated the mean age for people above 80 years old.




  mean_age mean_age_above_80 median_age   sd_age min_age max_age
1 58.82075          85.73333         55 9.499722      34     100

title: Data Summarization: Tables
text:
What are summary tables?

Summary tables are a way to present data in a structured format
The use is a little vague here…

It could mean:

A table for categorical data (like a frequency table)
A presentable table for categorical and numeric data



 

We will cover two functions that can help us create summary tables for categorical and numeric data:

tabyl() from the janitor package
tbl_summary() from the gtsummary package

title: Data Summarization: Tables
text:
What does tabyl() do?

tabyl() is a simple function that creates a frequency table for a single categorical variable
It returns a data frame with three columns:

n: the count in each category
percent: that count as a proportion of all rows (including missing values)
valid_percent: that count as a proportion of only the non-missing rows





Pretty simple to use and can be used to create two-by-two tables
Need to feed it one variable at a time

text:
What does tabyl() output look like?

  tabyl(degree)

text:
Cross-tabulations with tabyl()

You can also cross-tabulate two variables by adding a second column name

This will give you a table of counts for each combination of the two variables



hrs_00 |>
  tabyl(degree, sex)

                              degree Female Male
                 High school diploma    281  231
                     Master's degree    286  201
 Professional degree (Ph.D./M.D./JD)    115   79

                  Associate's degree    225  186

title: Data Summarization: Tables
text:
Example: Formatting a cross-tabulation

We can also add totals, convert to percentages, format as percents, and add counts back to a cross-tabulation


hrs_00 |>
1  tabyl(degree, sex) |>
2  adorn_totals(where = "row") |>
3  adorn_percentages(denominator = "col") |>
4  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 1) |>
5  adorn_ns(position = "front")


1

Create a cross-tabulation of degree by sex

2

Add a row for totals to the table. A little confusing because it totals each column.

3

Convert the counts to percentages, using the column totals (the added row of totals) as the denominator.

4

Format the percentages to 1 decimal place

5

Add the raw counts back to the table, in front of the percentages.

Example: Formatting a frequency table

We can add totals, convert to percentages, format as percents, and add counts back to a frequency table
Order matters!

You generally want: tabulate → add totals → convert to percentages → format as percents → add counts back

1  adorn_totals(where = "row") |>
2  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 2)

title: Data Summarization: Tables
text:
What does tbl_summary() do?

tbl_summary() builds a publication-ready summary table for all the columns you give it in a single command
It automatically picks sensible statistics based on each variable’s type:

Numeric variables: median (interquartile range)
Categorical variables: count (percent)
Missing values are shown as their own “Unknown” row

We need to use select() to decide what goes into the table

 



Great for publications!
You can customize the statistics shown, the labels, and even stratify the table by a grouping variable
Some of the customizations are syntax heavy
